**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 23, verses 1–2 (part 1 of 6):**

[Section: The difference between the humility (khushu') of faith and the humility of hypocrisy]

The difference between the humility of faith (khushu' al-iman) and the humility of hypocrisy (khushu' al-nifaq) is this. The humility of faith is the humility of the heart before Allah, through glorifying Him, revering Him, dignity, awe, and shame. The heart is broken before Allah with a broken state that is joined together by fear, shame, love, modesty, and witnessing Allah's blessings and His favours upon the servant. The heart is therefore certainly humble, and the humility of the limbs follows it. As for the humility of hypocrisy, it appears on the limbs as affectation and artificiality, while the heart is not humble.

One of the Companions used to say, "I seek refuge in Allah from the humility of hypocrisy." It was asked of him, "And what is the humility of hypocrisy?" He said, "That the body is seen to be humble while the heart is not humble."

So the one who is humble before Allah is a servant whose fires of desire have died down, and whose smoke has subsided from his chest. His chest is therefore opened and the light of Majesty shines within it. The desires of the soul die away out of the fear and gravity by which he is humbled. The limbs become still, the heart becomes dignified, and it is at rest with Allah and His remembrance, with the tranquility (sakinah) that has descended upon it from its Lord. It becomes humble (mukhbit) before Him. The mukhbit is the one who is at rest, for al-khabt (the lowland) of the earth is that which is level, so that water collects in it. Likewise the humble heart has become humbled and settled, like the level spot of earth to which water flows and in which it comes to rest. Its sign is that it prostrates before its Lord out of reverence for Him, and in abasement and submission before Him, a prostration from which it does not lift its head until it meets Him.

As for the arrogant heart, it has been shaken by its arrogance into a state of agitation, so it is like a raised mound of earth on which water does not settle. This is the humility of faith.

As for feigned lifelessness (al-tama'wut) and the humility of hypocrisy, it is a state in which the limbs are artificially kept still, in affectation and show-off, while the soul within is young, fresh, full of desires and wills. Such a person appears humble outwardly, like a snake of the valley or a lion of the thicket lying in wait between its flanks, waiting for its prey.

(Section)

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And establish the prayer﴾. So He commanded us to establish it, which means performing it upright and complete, with its standing, bowing, prostration, and remembrances. Allah, glory be to Him, has made success (al-falah) conditional upon the worshipper's humility in his prayer. Whoever loses the humility of prayer is not among the people of success. It is impossible for humility to be attained with haste and pecking, certainly. Indeed, humility is never attained except with tranquility (al-tuma'nina), and the more tranquil one is, the more humble he becomes. And the less humble one is, the more hasty he becomes, until his movements are like playing about that is not accompanied by humility, nor by turning toward worship, nor by knowledge of the true reality of servitude.

Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And establish the prayer﴾, and He said: ﴿Those who establish the prayer﴾, and He said: ﴿And establish the prayer﴾, and He said: ﴿So when you are at rest, then establish the prayer﴾, and He said: ﴿And those who establish prayer﴾. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said: ﴿My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer﴾, and He said to Musa: ﴿So worship Me and establish the prayer for My remembrance﴾. So you will hardly find mention of prayer in any place in the revelation except connected with establishing it. Those who perform prayer among people are few, and those who establish it among them are fewer still.

As 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The pilgrims are few, though the riders are many."

So those who act perform the commanded deeds carelessly, merely to fulfil the obligation, and they say, "The least that falls under the name suffices us, and we would that we performed it." If these people knew that the angels ascend with their prayer and present it to Allah, majestic and exalted, in the same way that gifts are presented by people to their kings and great ones seeking closeness to them, they would know that no one takes the best thing he can offer, beautifies it and perfects it as much as he can, and then draws near with it to one whom he hopes for and fears, the way someone takes the most worthless and lowest thing he has, so that he may be rid of it, and sends it to one who does not regard him at all. And it is not the one for whom prayer is the spring of his heart, his life, his rest, the coolness of his eye, the relief of his sorrow, the removal of his worry and grief, and his refuge in his calamities and trials, like the one for whom it is a burden on his limbs, an imposition, and a weight upon him. For the first, prayer is a great thing, yet the coolness of his eye and his rest; for the second, it is a heavy burden.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer, and indeed it is difficult except for the humble, who are certain that they will meet their Lord and that to Him they will return﴾. It is only difficult for others because their hearts are empty of love for Allah the Exalted, of exalting and magnifying Him, of humility before Him, and because of their little desire for Him. Indeed, the servant's presence in prayer, his humility within it, his completion of it, and his exertion and effort in establishing and completing it, are in proportion to his desire for Allah the Exalted.

Imam Ahmad said, in the narration of Mahna ibn Yahya: "Their share of Islam is in proportion to their share of prayer, and their desire for Islam is in proportion to their desire for prayer. So know yourself, O servant of Allah, and beware of meeting Allah, mighty and majestic, while Islam has no measure in your heart. For the measure of Islam in your heart is like the measure of prayer in your heart."

The share of a heart filled with love of Allah, fear of Him, desire for Him, and reverence and magnification of Him, from prayer, is not like the share of an empty, ruined heart devoid of these. So when two people stand before Allah in prayer, this one stands with a heart that is humble and submissive to Him, close to Him, sound and free from evil intrusions. Its spaces are filled with awe, the light of faith shines within it, the veil of the soul and the smoke of desires are lifted from it, and so it frolics in the gardens of the meanings of the Qur'an. The sweetness of faith mingles in his heart with the true realities of the Names and Attributes, their exaltedness, beauty, and supreme perfection, and the uniqueness of the Lord, glory be to Him, in the descriptions of His majesty and the attributes of His perfection. So his aspiration is gathered upon Allah, his eye is cooled by Him, and he perceives His nearness with a nearness that has no equal. So his heart is emptied for Him and turns to Him with all of its being. This turning of his is between two turnings from his Lord, for He, glory be to Him, first turned to him, so his heart was drawn to Him by His turning. Then, when he turned to his Lord, he received from Him another turning, more complete than the first.

Here is a wonder from the wonders of the Names and Attributes, which occurs to one whose heart understands the meanings of the Qur'an and in whose heart the sweetness of faith has mingled with them, to the degree that he sees for each Name and Attribute a place and station within his prayer. When he stands upright before the Lord, blessed and exalted, he witnesses in his heart His self-subsistence (qayyumiyyah). When he says "Allahu akbar," he witnesses His greatness. When he says, "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You; blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god other than You," he witnesses in his heart a Lord free of every defect, clear of every imperfection, praised with every praise. His praise includes the description of Him with every perfection, and that necessitates His freedom from every imperfection, blessed is His name. So nothing is mentioned over a little except that it becomes abundant, nothing over good except that He increases it and blesses it, nothing over a calamity except that He removes it, nothing over a devil except that He turns it back, humiliated and repelled. The perfection of the Name is from the perfection of the One named. So if the state of His Name is such that nothing on earth or in heaven can harm one who invokes it, then the state of the One named is higher and more majestic.

(And exalted is His majesty) means that His greatness has risen high and is glorified above every greatness, His rank is exalted above every rank, and His authority has overcome every authority. So He is exalted above having any partner in His dominion and lordship, in His divinity, in His acts, or in His attributes, as the jinn believer said: ﴿And indeed, exalted is the majesty of our Lord; He has not taken a wife nor a son﴾. How many revelations of the realities of the Names and Attributes are there in these words, upon the heart of one who knows them, without nullifying their realities (ta'til). And when he says, "I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan," he has taken refuge in his strong corner and sought protection by Allah's power and strength from his enemy, who wants to cut him off from his Lord and remove him from His nearness, so that he may be in a worse state.

"When he says: ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, he pauses briefly, waiting for his Lord's response to him, saying: 'My servant has praised Me.'

When he says: ﴿The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾, he waits for the answer, 'My servant has extolled Me.' When he says: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾, he waits for His answer: 'My servant has glorified Me.' How delightful for his heart, how cool for his eye, and how joyful for his soul is his Lord's saying, 'My servant,' three times! By Allah, were it not for the smoke of desires that is upon the hearts and the clouds of the souls, they would fly away with joy and delight at the words of their Lord, their Creator, and their Worshipped One: 'My servant has praised Me, My servant has extolled Me, and My servant has glorified Me.'

Then his heart has room to witness these three Names, which are the foundations of the Most Beautiful Names: Allah, the Lord, and the Most Merciful. His heart witnesses from the mention of the Name Allah, blessed and exalted, the God who is worshipped, existing, and feared, who does not deserve worship other than Him and to whom worship alone is fitting. Faces are humbled before Him, existing things submit to Him, and voices are humbled before Him: ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whatever is in them glorify Him, and there is not a thing except that it glorifies Him with praise﴾, and ﴿To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him﴾.

Likewise, He created the heavens and the earth and what is between them, He created the jinn, mankind, birds, beasts, Paradise, and Hellfire. Likewise, He sent the messengers, revealed the books, legislated the laws, and obligated His servants with command and prohibition. And he witnesses that the One whose name is "Lord of the worlds" is Self-Subsisting (qayyum). He subsists by Himself, and everything subsists by Him. He is Guardian over every soul in its good and its evil. He has established Himself upon His Throne and has singled Himself out in the management of His dominion.

So the entire management is in His hand, and the outcome of all affairs returns to Him. The decrees of management descend from Him through His angels, with giving and withholding, lowering and raising, giving life and causing death, repentance and dismissal, restraint and expansion, the relief of distress, the aid of the afflicted, and the answering of those in need: ﴿Whoever is in the heavens and the earth asks Him; every day He is in a matter﴾. There is none who can withhold what He gives, none who can give what He withholds, none who can reverse His judgment, none who can repel His command, and none who can change His words. The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him, and deeds are presented to Him at the beginning and end of the day. He decrees the measures, sets the appointed times, and drives the measures to their appointed times, standing in charge of all of this, its preservation and its interests.

Then, when he mentions the Name the Most Merciful, majestic is His majesty, he witnesses a Lord who does good to His creation with every kind of goodness, who makes Himself beloved to them with all kinds of blessings. His mercy and knowledge encompass everything, and He has granted every creature abundant blessing and favour. So His mercy encompassed everything, and His blessing encompassed every living being. His mercy extends wherever His knowledge extends. He established Himself upon His Throne by His mercy, created His creation by His mercy, revealed His books by His mercy, sent His messengers by His mercy, legislated His laws by His mercy, and created Paradise by His mercy, and the Fire too is by His mercy, for it is His whip with which He drives His believing servants to His Paradise, and by which He purifies the impurities of the monotheists among the people of His disobedience, and it is His prison in which He imprisons whom He wills of His creation.

So contemplate what is in His command, His prohibition, His counsels, and His admonitions of profound mercy and all-encompassing blessing, and what is within their folds of mercy and blessing. Mercy is the connecting cause from Him to His servants, just as servitude is the connecting cause from them to Him. From them to Him is servitude, and from Him to them is mercy. Among the most special witnessings of this Name is the witnessing by the one who prays of his share of mercy by which He has established him before his Lord, and has qualified him for His servitude and intimate conversation, and given him what He withheld from others. He turned his heart toward Him and turned others' hearts away, and that is from His mercy toward him.

When he says: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾, here he witnesses the glory that does not befit anyone but the true, manifest King. So he witnesses a dominant King, to whom creation has submitted, before whom faces are humbled, before whose greatness the tyrants are humbled, and before whose might every mighty one submits. He witnesses in his heart a King upon the Throne of heaven, dominant by His might, before whom faces bow and prostrate. If the reality of the attribute of kingship is not nullified, it reveals to him the witnessing of the realities of the Names and Attributes, for nullifying them is a nullification of His kingship and a denial of it. The true, complete King cannot be anything but living, self-subsisting, all-hearing, all-seeing, governing, all-powerful, speaking, commanding, forbidding, established upon the throne of His kingdom, sending His messengers to the farthest reaches of His dominion with His commands. He is pleased with those who deserve pleasure, rewards them, honours them, and brings them near. He is angry with those who deserve anger, punishes them, humiliates them, and distances them. He punishes whom He wills, shows mercy to whom He wills, gives to whom He wills, brings near whom He wills, and distances whom He wills. He has an abode of punishment, which is the Fire, and He has an abode of great happiness, which is Paradise.

So whoever nullifies any of this, or denies it, or rejects its reality, has indeed impugned His kingship, glory be to Him and exalted, and negated His perfection and completeness.

Likewise, whoever denies the comprehensiveness of His decree and destiny has denied the comprehensiveness of His kingship and perfection. So the one who prays witnesses the glory of the Lord, exalted, in His saying: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾. When he says: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾, in it is the secret of creation and command, of this world and the Hereafter. It includes the most sublime ends and the best means. The most sublime of ends is His servitude, and the best of means is His help. So there is no deity deserving worship except Him, and no helper in His worship other than Him. So His worship is the highest of ends, and His help is the most sublime of means. Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, sent down one hundred and four books, and the meanings of them were gathered into four: the Torah, the Gospel, the Qur'an, and the Psalms. The meanings of these four were gathered into the Qur'an, the meanings of the Qur'an were gathered into the mufassal (the short surahs), the meanings of the mufassal were gathered into al-Fatihah, and the meanings of al-Fatihah were gathered into: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾. This phrase encompasses the two kinds of tawhid (oneness of God): tawhid al-rububiyyah (oneness of Lordship) and tawhid al-uluhiyyah (oneness of divinity). It includes worship by the Name "Lord" and the Name "Allah." He is worshipped by His divinity, He is sought for help by His lordship, and He guides to the straight path by His mercy. So the beginning of the surah mentioned His Names: Allah, the Lord, and the Most Merciful, corresponding to the one seeking worship, help, and guidance. He alone grants all of that. None assists in His worship but Him, and none guides but Him.

Then the supplicant witnesses, in his saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, his intense need and his dependence on this request, than which he has no greater need or necessity at all, for he needs it in every breath and every blink of an eye.

This requested thing in this supplication is not completed except by guidance to the path that leads to Him, glory be to Him. That guidance includes the guidance of detail, the creation of the power to act, its will, its formation, and His granting success so that it is done in the manner pleasing and beloved to the Lord, glory be to Him and exalted, and His preserving it from its corruptions during and after the act. Since the servant is in need of this guidance in every state, regarding all that he does and abandons, from matters that he has done without guidance, he needs to repent of them; from matters in which he was guided to their root but not their details, or guided to them partially and not wholly, he needs to complete the guidance in them so that he may increase in guidance; from matters in which he needs for the future the same guidance he received in the past; from matters in which he is devoid of correct belief, he needs guidance in them; from matters he has not performed, he needs to perform them in the manner of guidance; and from matters in which he has been guided to the true belief and right action, he needs steadfastness upon them.

Along with the other kinds of guidance, Allah, glory be to Him, has obligated him to ask for this guidance in his best states, many times a day and a night. Then He explained that the people of this guidance are those singled out for His blessing, not those who have incurred anger, who are those who knew the truth and did not follow it, nor the misguided, who are those who worshipped Allah without knowledge. The two groups share in speaking about His creation, His command, His names and His attributes without knowledge. So the path of the one blessed is distinct from the path of the people of falsehood, in knowledge and in action, entirely.

When he finished this praise, supplication, and tawhid, it was prescribed for him to seal all of this with a seal of saying "Amin," which is like a ring upon it, in which he agrees with the angels of heaven. This saying of "Amin" is part of the adornment of prayer, like the raising of the hands, which is also an adornment of prayer, and a following of the Sunnah, a glorification of Allah's command, a servitude of the hands, and a sign of moving from one pillar to another. Then he begins to converse intimately with his Lord with His words, and to listen, when the imam recites, with attentive silence and presence of heart and witnessing.

The best of the remembrances of prayer is the remembrance in standing, and the best posture of the one praying is the posture of standing. So it is singled out for praise, glorification, and magnification, and the recitation of the speech of the Lord, majestic is He. For this reason, reciting the Qur'an in bowing and prostration was forbidden, because these two are states of humiliation, submission, lowliness and lowering. For this reason, the remembrances that suit their postures were prescribed in them. So the one bowing is prescribed to mention the greatness of his Lord in his own state of lowering, bending, and submission, and that He, glory be to Him, is described with the description of His greatness, above anything that contradicts His pride, majesty, and greatness. So the best thing the one bowing says in absolute terms is: "Glory be to my Lord, the Mighty." For Allah, glory be to Him, commanded the servants with this, and the messenger who conveyed from Him, the emissary between Him and His servants, specified this place for this remembrance when the verse was revealed: ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾, and he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace (ﷺ), said: "Make it in your bowing."

(Section)

Many scholars have held that the prayer of one who deliberately omits bowing is invalid, and that one who omits it through forgetfulness must perform the prostration of forgetfulness (sujud al-sahw, the prostration performed to correct an error in prayer). This is the view of Imam Ahmad and those who agreed with him among the imams of hadith and the Sunnah. The command to bow is no less binding than the command to send blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ) in the final tashahhud (the seated testimony of faith), and its obligation is no less than the obligation of the worshipper placing his forehead and hands on the ground. Bowing (ruku') is the glorification of the Lord, may His majesty be exalted, with the heart, the body, and the tongue. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "As for bowing, glorify the Lord therein."

(Section)

Then the worshipper raises his head, returning to the completion of his remembrance. The emblem of this pillar is the praise of God, extolling Him and magnifying Him. The worshipper opens this emblem with his saying: "God hears whoever praises Him" (sami'a Allahu liman hamidah), meaning: He hears with a hearing of acceptance and response. Then he follows it with: "Our Lord, and to You belongs praise, filling the heavens and filling the earth, and filling whatever is between them, and filling whatever else You will" (rabbana wa-laka al-hamd, mil' al-samawati wa-mil' al-ard, wa-mil' ma baynahuma, wa-mil' ma shi'ta min shay'). The letter waw (and) in his saying "Our Lord, and to You belongs praise" must not be neglected, for its use has been recommended in the two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim). It makes the speech, in its implied sense, two independent sentences. His saying "Our Lord" implicitly includes the meaning: You are the Lord, the King, the Self-Subsisting, in whose hand are the reins of all affairs and to whom they all return. Then he adds to this understood meaning his saying "and to You belongs praise," which contains the meaning of the monotheist's saying: "To Him belongs the dominion, and to Him belongs the praise." Then he speaks of the greatness of this praise in its magnitude and its quality, saying: "filling the heavens and filling the earth, and filling whatever is between them, and filling whatever else You will." That is, its measure is the measure of filling the upper world, the lower world, and the space between them. This praise has filled the existing creation, and it fills what the Lord, blessed and exalted, will create afterwards, of whatever He wills. So His praise has filled every existing thing and has filled what will exist. This is the better of the two interpretations. It has also been said that "whatever else You will" refers to what lies beyond the world, so that the later phrase "of time" would correspond to the first interpretation and "of place" to the second.

Then he follows this with: "Worthy of praise and glory" (ahl al-thana' wa'l-majd), so the matter returns after the bowing to what he opened the prayer with before the bowing: praise, extolling, and glory. Then he follows it with: "Most truly has the servant spoken" (ahaqq ma qala al-'abd), affirming His praise, His glorification, and His extolling, and that this is the truest thing a servant can utter. Then he follows it with the acknowledgement of servitude, that this is a general ruling for all servants. Then he concludes that with: "No one can withhold what You give, and no one can give what You withhold, and no fortune can benefit its possessor against You" (la mani'a lima a'tayta wa-la mu'ti lima mana'ta wa-la yanfa'u dha'l-jaddi minka al-jadd).

He used to say this also after the completion of the prayer. He says it in these two places as an acknowledgement of His oneness and that all blessings come from Him. This includes several matters. The first: He alone gives and withholds. The second: when He gives, no one can prevent what He has given, and when He withholds, no one can give to one whom He has withheld from. The third: the fortunes of the sons of Adam, and their portions of dominion, leadership, wealth, pleasant living, and other things, do not benefit them with Him, nor do they save them from His punishment or bring them nearer to His honor. Only drawing near to Him through obedience and preferring His good pleasure benefits them with Him.

Then he concludes that with: "O God, wash me of my sins with water, snow and hail" (Allahumma'ghsilni min khataya ya bi'l-ma'i wa'l-thalji wa'l-barad), just as he began the rak'ah with it at the beginning of the opening supplication (istiftah). Just as he used to end the prayer with seeking forgiveness, and seeking forgiveness was at the beginning, middle, and end of the prayer, this pillar includes the best of remembrances and the most beneficial of supplications: praising Him, glorifying Him, extolling Him, acknowledging to Him servitude and His oneness, and disavowing one's sins and faults before Him. It is therefore a remembrance intended within a pillar intended, not less than the bowing and the prostration.

(Section)

Then he says "God is greatest" and falls into prostration to God, not raising his hands, because the hands descend for prostration just as the face descends. They descend in their servitude, so this makes raising them unnecessary. For this reason raising them has not been prescribed. Then he raises his head from prostration, for the hands are raised with it just as they are placed down with it. Prostration was prescribed in its most perfect form, in its strongest expression of servitude, and in its most comprehensive form for all the limbs, such that every part of the body takes its share of servitude. Prostration is the secret of the prayer, its greatest pillar, and the conclusion of the rak'ah. What precedes it of the pillars is like preliminaries to it. It resembles the circumambulation of visitation (tawaf al-ziyarah) in the Hajj, for that is the intended goal of the Hajj, the place of entering into the presence of God and visiting Him, while what precedes it is like preliminaries to it. For this reason the servant is nearest to his Lord when he is in prostration, and the best state for him is the state in which he is nearest to God. For this reason supplication in this position is closer to being answered.

When God, glorified be He, created the servant from the earth, he was worthy of not departing from his origin, but of returning to it when his nature and soul urge him to depart from it. If the servant were left to his nature and the impulses of his soul, he would become arrogant, exult, depart from his origin from which he was created, and rush to snatch from his Lord the qualities of greatness and magnificence, contending with Him for them. So he was commanded to prostrate, in submission to the majesty of his Lord, in humility before Him, in abasement before Him, and in lowliness. This humility, submission, and abasement returns him to the rule of servitude and makes up for the lapse, heedlessness, and turning away that had taken him out of his origin. The reality of the dust from which he was created is thus represented to him, as he places upon it the most noble and highest part of himself, which is the face. Its highest part has become its lowest, in submission before his Most High Lord, in humility before Him, in lowliness before His greatness, and in self-abasement before His might. This is the utmost of outward humility. God, glorified be He, created him from the earth, which is made low for treading upon by the feet, and He employed him upon it, returned him to it, and promised him that He would bring him out of it. So it is his mother and his father, his origin and his offspring. It has held him alive upon its back and dead within it, and has been made for him a purity and a place of prostration. So He commanded prostration, for it is the utmost of outward humility, and it gathers servitude for all the limbs. So he rubs his face in the dust in self-abasement, humility, submission, and casting down of his hands.

Masruq said to Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "Nothing remains that one would desire except that we rub our faces in the dust before Him." The Prophet (ﷺ) did not intentionally guard his face from the ground; rather, when that happened to him, he did it. For this reason he prostrated in water and mud. This is why among the perfections of the obligatory prostration is that one prostrates upon the seven limbs: the face, the two hands, the two knees, and the tips of the two feet. This is an obligation that God commanded and that His Messenger conveyed to his community.

Among its obligatory or recommended perfections is placing the prayer place with the surface of the face and resting upon the ground, such that the weight of the head reaches the ground and the lower parts are raised above the upper parts. This is part of the completion of prostration. Among its perfection is that it takes a form in which each limb of the body takes its share of humility: the stomach is kept away from the thighs, the thighs from the shins, the upper arms are kept away from the sides, and they are not spread flat upon the ground, so that each limb may stand independently in servitude.

For this reason, when Satan sees the son of Adam prostrating to God, he withdraws to a side, weeping, and says: "Woe is me! The son of Adam was commanded to prostrate, so he prostrated, and for him is Paradise. I was commanded to prostrate, but I disobeyed, and for me is the Fire."

For this reason God praised those who fall down in prostration when they hear His speech, and blamed those who do not fall prostrate before it. For this reason the view of one who made it obligatory is strong in its evidence. When the magicians recognized the truth of Musa (Moses) and the falsehood of Fir'awn (Pharaoh), they fell down prostrate before their Lord, and that prostration was the first of their happiness and the forgiveness of what they had spent their lives on of magic.

For this reason God informed of the prostration of all creatures to Him, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To God prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of living creatures, and the angels, and they are not arrogant. They fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are commanded.﴾ He informed of their faith in His loftiness and His supremacy, and of their submission to Him through prostration in glorification and reverence. He also said, may He be exalted: ﴿Do you not see that to God prostrates whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun, and the moon, and the stars, and the mountains, and the trees, and the animals, and many of mankind? And many have deserved the punishment. And whoever God humiliates, there is none to honor him. Indeed, God does what He wills.﴾

So the one upon whom the punishment has been decreed is the one who does not prostrate to Him, glorified be He, and He has humiliated him by his abandoning prostration to Him. He informed that there is no one to honor him, and he has been humiliated before his Lord since he did not prostrate to Him. He also said: ﴿To God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly, and their shadows at morning and evening.﴾

Since servitude is the ultimate perfection of man and his nearness to God is according to his share of servitude, and since the prayer gathers the scattered forms of servitude and includes their divisions, it is the best of the servant's deeds, and its rank in Islam is like the rank of the central pole of a tent.

Prostration is the best of its physical pillars and its secret, for which it was prescribed. Its repetition in the prayer is more than the repetition of the other pillars. He made it the conclusion of the rak'ah and its goal. Its performance was prescribed after the bowing, for bowing is a preparation for it and an introduction before it. In it is prescribed the praise of God that befits it, which is the servant's saying: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High" (subhana rabbiya al-a'la). This is the best that can be said in it. No command from the Prophet (ﷺ) to say anything else in prostration has been reported, when he said: "Make it in your prostrations." Whoever abandons it deliberately, his prayer is invalid according to many scholars, among them Imam Ahmad and others, because he has not done what he was commanded. The description of the Lord as Most High in this state is most fitting for the state of the one prostrating who has lowered himself to the bottom, upon his face. He mentions the loftiness of his Lord in the state of his falling, just as he mentioned His greatness in the state of his humility in bowing, and he exalts his Lord above what does not befit Him and what contradicts His greatness and His loftiness.

Then, since prostration is prescribed in a repeated form, there was no alternative but to separate the two prostrations. So he separated them with a pillar intended in itself, in which is prescribed the supplication that suits it and fits it, which is the servant's request for forgiveness, mercy, guidance, well-being, and provision. These include bringing about the good of this world and the next and repelling the evil of this world and the next. Mercy brings about good, forgiveness protects from evil, guidance leads to both, and provision is the giving of what sustains the body, such as food and drink, and what sustains the soul and heart, such as knowledge and faith. The sitting between the prostrations is made the place for this supplication, because of what precedes it of God's mercy, praise of Him, and humility before Him. This was a means for the supplicant and an introduction before his need. So this pillar is the intended place for supplication in it. It is a pillar set for desire and for seeking pardon, forgiveness, and mercy. When the servant has performed standing, praise, extolling, and glorification, then humility, exalting and glorifying the Lord, then has returned to praise and extolling, and then completed all that with the utmost lowliness, humility, and submission, there remains the request for his need, his apology, and his disavowal. So it is prescribed for him to take the form of one who serves, so he sits as the lowly servant sits, kneeling on his knees, like one who casts himself before his master, hoping and fearing, apologizing to him, and seeking his help against his commanding self that inclines to evil.

Then he is prescribed to repeat this servitude time after time until he completes the four rak'ahs, just as he is prescribed to repeat the remembrance time after time, because that is more effective in achieving the goal and more conducive to submission and humility. When he has completed the bowing, prostration, recitation, and glorification of the prayer, then he is prescribed to sit at the end of his prayer in a sitting of one who is humbled, abased, and submissive, kneeling on his knees. In this sitting he recites the most complete and best of the greetings (al-tahiyyat) in place of the greeting of a created being to another created being when he meets him or enters upon him. People greet their kings and nobles with various kinds of greetings by which they greet their hearts. Some say: "Good morning." Some say: "To you be permanence and blessing." Some say: "May God prolong your life." Some say: "May you live a thousand years." Some prostrate before kings, and some offer greeting. So their greetings among themselves include what the one greeted loves of sayings and actions. The polytheists greet their idols.

Al-Hasan (al-Basri) said: "The people of ignorance used to rub themselves against their idols and say: 'To you belongs everlasting life.' When Islam came, they were commanded to make the best, purest, and most excellent of those greetings belong to God. The greeting is the greeting of the servant to the Living who does not die, and He, glorified be He, is more worthy of those greetings than anything else, for they include life, permanence, and everlastingness. No one deserves these greetings except the Living, the Everlasting, who does not die and whose dominion does not cease." Likewise His saying: "and the prayers" (wa'l-salawat), for no one deserves prayer except God, mighty and majestic, and to offer prayer to other than Him is among the greatest disbelief and association with Him. Likewise His saying: "and the good things" (wa'l-tayyibat): it is a description of a noun that has been omitted, meaning the good words, actions, attributes, and names belong to God alone. He is good, His acts are good, His attributes are the best of things, His names are the best of names, and His name is "the Good." Nothing proceeds from Him except what is good, nothing ascends to Him except what is good, and nothing draws near to Him except what is good. To Him ascends the good word, and the good deed rises to Him. So all good things belong to Him, are attributed to Him, proceed from Him, and terminate in Him.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God is good and accepts only what is good." In the hadith of the incantation for the sick, narrated by Abu Dawud (number omitted) and others: "You are the Lord of the good, and none who are good draw near to Him from among His servants." Just as it is said to the people of Paradise: ﴿Peace be upon you; you have become good, so enter it, abiding forever.﴾ God, may He be exalted, has decreed in His law and His decree that good things are for the good. If He, glorified be He, is the Good in the absolute sense, then the good words, good actions, good attributes, and good names all belong to Him, glorified be He, and no one deserves them besides Him. Rather, nothing has ever been good except by His goodness, glorified be He, so the goodness of everything other than Him is one of the traces of His goodness. This good greeting is suitable for none but Him.

Since the salam (peace) is one kind of greeting, and the Muslim is supplicating for the one he greets, and since God, glorified be He, is the One from whom peace is requested for His servants whom He has chosen for His servitude and whom He has accepted for Himself, it was prescribed that the greeting begin with the most honored of them before Him, the most beloved to Him, and the nearest to Him in rank, namely by the two testimonies which are the key to Islam. So it was prescribed that it be the conclusion of the prayer. The worshipper entered it with the takbir (saying "God is greatest"), praise, extolling, and glorification, and the affirmation of God's lordship and divinity, and concluded it with the testimony that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger.

This greeting was prescribed in the middle of the prayer when it exceeds two rak'ahs, likening it to the sitting between the prostrations. In it, together with the separation, there is rest for the worshper, so that he approaches the last two rak'ahs with energy and strength, unlike when he joins the rak'ahs without a break. For this reason the better practice in voluntary prayer is two by two, and if one performs four voluntary rak'ahs, he sits in the middle of them.

(Section)

The words of the tashahhud were placed at the end of the prayer in the position of the khutbat al-hajah (the sermon of need) that precedes a request. When the worshipper has finished his prayer, he sits in the sitting of one who desires and fears, asking his Lord for what he cannot do without. So before his petition, the words of the greeting are prescribed for him as an introduction before his request. Then he follows it with blessings upon the one through whom his community received this blessing and felicity. It is as if the worshipper seeks a means to God, glorified be He, through his servitude, then through praise of Him, and then through testifying to His oneness and to His Messenger's prophethood. Then he sends blessings upon His Messenger. Then he is told: choose from among the supplications the one you love most, for that is the right that is upon you, and this is the right that is yours.

The blessings upon his family (ali) were prescribed along with the blessings upon him, to complete the coolness of his eyes by honoring his family and sending blessings upon them, and that he should send blessings upon him and upon his family as He sent blessings upon his father Ibrahim (Abraham) and his family. All the prophets after Ibrahim are of his family. For this reason what was sought for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is blessings like the blessings upon Ibrahim and upon all the prophets after him and the believing family. For this reason this blessing is the most complete and the most excellent with which one sends blessings upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ). When the worshipper has offered it, he is commanded to seek refuge in God from all forms of evil, for evil is either the punishment of the Hereafter or its cause. So evil is only the punishment and its causes. The punishment is of two kinds: punishment in the barzakh (the intermediate realm) and punishment in the Hereafter. Its causes are trials, which are of two kinds: the greater and the lesser. The greater trial is the trial of the Dajjal (Antichrist) and the trial of death. The lesser trial is the trial of life, which can be remedied by repentance, unlike the trial of death and the trial of the Dajjal, for the one afflicted by them cannot remedy them.

Then he is prescribed from among the supplications what he chooses concerning the benefits of his worldly life and his Hereafter. Supplication in this place before the salam is better than supplication after the salam, and more beneficial for the one who supplicates. Likewise, most of the supplications of the Prophet (ﷺ) were in the prayer from its beginning to its end. He used to supplicate in the opening supplication with various kinds of supplication, after the bowing, after raising his head from it, in prostration, between the two prostrations, and in the tashahhud before the salam. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may God be pleased with him) was taught a supplication to say in his prayer, and al-Hasan ibn Ali was taught a supplication to recite in the qunut (supplication) of the witr prayer.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 23, verses 1–2 (part 3 of 6):

It was his practice that when he supplicated for a people or against a people, he would do so in the prayer after the bowing (ruku'). Among this is that the one praying, before his salam, is in the place of intimate conversation and nearness before his Lord, so supplication in this state is closer to being answered than supplication after he has departed from before Him. The Prophet ﷺ was asked, "Which supplication is most likely to be heard?" and he said: "The middle of the night and the end of the obligatory prayers." The *dubur* (end, last part) of the prayer is its final portion, like the *dubur* of an animal or the back of a wall. The *dubur* of the prayer may also refer to what comes after its conclusion, when there is an indication that shows this, as in his saying: "Glorify Allah, praise Him, and magnify Him, *dubur* of every prayer, thirty-three times each." Here *dubur* means the completion of the prayer. This is similar to the expiry of a term (ajal): the term is said to have its last part and is also said to have reached its end and conclusion.

(Section)

Then the prayer is concluded with the salam, and it is made the *tahlil* (release, the act by which one exits the state of prayer), by which the one praying leaves it, just as one leaves the state of ihram of Hajj by the *tahlil* of Hajj. The imam's *tahlil* is a supplication by him for those behind him for safety (*salamah*), which is the root and foundation of all good. So it was prescribed for those behind him to make their *tahlil* in the same way as the imam made his, and in this there is a supplication for him and for those praying with him for peace. Then this was prescribed for every worshipper, even if he prays alone, for there is no better release from the prayer than this. Just as there is no better opening of it than the *takbir* as its *tahrim* (the act that makes it forbidden to do otherwise), so its *tahrim* is the magnifying of the Lord, Exalted is He, which combines affirming every perfection for Him, declaring Him free of every deficiency and defect, singling Him out and specifying Him with this, and exalting and glorifying Him. The *takbir* includes the details of the prayer's actions, words and forms, so the prayer from beginning to end is an elaboration of the content of "Allahu Akbar." What *tahrim* could be better than this *tahrim*, which contains sincerity (*ikhlas*) and monotheism (*tawhid*)? And this *tahlil* contains beneficence toward one's believing brothers. Thus it opens with sincerity and closes with beneficence.

He said in the book (*al-Kalam ʿala Masʾalat al-Sama'*):

Then He prescribed for them the raising of the hands at the bowing, as a glorification of Allah's command, an adornment of the prayer, and a special servitude of the hands like the servitude of the rest of the limbs, and as following the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. So it is the ornament of the prayer, its adornment, and a magnification of its rites.

Then He prescribed the *takbir*, which occurs in the transitions of the prayer from one pillar to another, like the *talbiyah* in the transitions of the pilgrim from one station (mash'ar) to another. So it is the emblem of the prayer, just as the talbiyah is the emblem of Hajj, so that the servant may know that the secret of the prayer is the magnifying of the Lord, Exalted is He, and glorifying Him by worshipping Him alone.

Then He prescribed for him to humble himself before the Worshipped, glorified is He, by bowing, in humility before His greatness, submission to His awe, and lowliness before His might. So the servant bends his spine for Him, sets his stature for Him, lowers his head for Him, and bows his back for Him, magnifying Him and speaking His glorification together with His magnification. Thus there gathers for him the humility of the heart, the humility of the limbs, and the humility of speech, in the most complete state. In this dhikr he combined humility and magnification toward his Lord, and the declaration of His freedom from the humility of servants, for humility is the attribute of the servant and greatness is the attribute of the Lord.

The perfection of the servitude of bowing is that the servant become small and diminished, such that his diminishing erases every magnification of himself, and establishes in its place the magnification of his Lord. Whenever the magnifying of the Lord takes hold of his heart, his own smallness in his own eyes increases. So bowing belongs primarily and intentionally to the heart, and to the limbs by way of consequence and completion.

Then He prescribed for him to praise his Lord and extol Him for His blessings when he rises and stands upright, returning to his best posture, erect and balanced in stature. He praises his Lord and extols Him for having enabled him to that humility, then moved him from it to the station of standing and balance before Him, standing in His service. Just as in the state of recitation, this standing has a special savour and a state that arises in the heart distinct from the savour and state of bowing. It is a pillar intended for its own sake, the same as the pillar of bowing and prostration. For this reason the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would prolong it as he prolonged bowing and prostration, and he would increase in it praise, glorification and exaltation, as we have mentioned in his guidance ﷺ. In night prayer he would repeat often, "To my Lord is the praise, to my Lord is the praise."

Then He prescribed for him to say the *takbir* and fall down prostrate. In his prostration he gives every limb its share of servitude. He places his forehead on the ground before his Lord, pressing it down, rubbing his nose in dust before Him, his heart humbled to Him. He places the noblest part of himself, which is his face, upon the ground, especially upon dust, rubbing it before his Master, rubbing his nose, his heart and limbs humbled to Him, submitting to His greatness, bowing to His might, humbled before Him. He is the most abased and most broken of things before his Lord, Exalted is He, glorifying Him for His exaltation within his utmost lowliness, his upper parts turned down to his lower parts in abasement, submission and brokenness. His heart has conformed to the state of his body, so the heart prostrates as the face prostrates. His nose, his hands, his knees and his feet prostrate with it. He prescribed that he lift his thighs from his shins, his belly from his thighs, and his elbows from his sides, so that every part of him takes its share of humility, and no part bears another. It is most fitting in this state that he be nearer to his Lord than in other states, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating." Since the prostration of the heart is its complete submission to its Lord, it is possible to continue this prostration until the day one meets Him. As it was said to one of the early generations: "Does the heart prostrate?" He said: "Yes, by Allah! A prostration from which he does not lift his head until he meets Allah."

Since the prayer was built on five: the recitation, the standing, the bowing, the prostration and the dhikr, it was named after each of these five. It was called *qiyam* (standing), as in His saying: ﴿Stand [in prayer] at night, except a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 2], and His saying: ﴿And stand before Allah devoutly obedient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238]. It was called *qira'ah* (recitation), as in His saying: ﴿And the recitation of dawn; indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed﴾ [al-Isra': 78]. It was called *ruku'* (bowing), as in His saying: ﴿And bow with those who bow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 43], and His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow," they do not bow﴾ [al-Mursalat: 48]. It was called *sujud* (prostration), as in His saying: ﴿So glorify with the praise of your Lord and be among those who prostrate﴾ [al-Hijr: 98], and His saying: ﴿No! Do not obey him, but prostrate and draw near﴾ [al-'Alaq: 19]. It was called *dhikr* (remembrance), as in His saying: ﴿When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday, then hasten to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 9], and His saying: ﴿Let not your wealth or your children divert you from the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 9]. The noblest of its actions is the prostration, and the noblest of its invocations is the recitation. The first surah revealed to the Prophet ﷺ began with recitation and ended with prostration, and the rak'ah was constructed upon this: its beginning is recitation and its end is prostration.

Then He prescribed for him to raise his head and sit upright. Since this sitting is enclosed between two prostrations, one before it and one after it, moving from prostration to it and then from it to prostration, it has its own significance.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ would prolong it to the length of the prostration, and in it he would plead humbly to his Lord and seek His forgiveness, asking Him for His mercy, guidance, provision and well-being. It has a special savour and a state of the heart distinct from the savour and state of prostration. In this sitting the servant has taken the form of one kneeling before his Lord, casting himself before Him, apologising to Him for what he has committed, desiring that He forgive him and have mercy on him, seeking aid against his own commanding soul (*nafs ammarah*). The Prophet ﷺ would repeat the seeking of forgiveness in this sitting and increase his longing for Allah in it.

So picture yourself as a debtor who owes the right of Allah, while you are the guarantor of it, and the debtor is evasive and deceitful. You are being pursued on the guarantee, and the debtor is being pursued for the right, so you seek aid against him until you extract what is owed from him to free yourself from the demand. The heart is the partner of the soul in good and evil, reward and punishment, praise and blame. The soul's nature is to flee and to leave the bondage of servitude and to squander the rights of Allah that are due. The heart is its partner, and if its authority grows strong, it becomes its captive, and it is the partner and captive of the soul if the soul's authority grows strong.

So He prescribed for the servant, when he raises his head from prostration, to kneel before Allah seeking aid against his own soul, apologising to his Lord for what it has done, desiring that He have mercy on him, forgive him, guide him, provide for him and grant him well-being. These five are the sum of the good of this world and the Hereafter, for the servant is in need, indeed compelled, to secure his benefits in this world and the Hereafter and to ward off harms from himself in this world and the Hereafter. This supplication includes them all: provision brings him the benefits of his worldly life, well-being repels its harms, guidance brings him the benefits of his next life, forgiveness repels its harms, and mercy encompasses all of that.

He prescribed for him to return to prostration as he was before, and not to suffice with a single prostration in the rak'ah as he sufficed with a single bowing, because of the excellence and nobility of prostration, its station with Allah, and that He is nearest to His servant while he is prostrating. It is more deeply rooted in servitude and more firmly established in it than anything else. For this reason it was made the conclusion of the rak'ah, and what precedes it is like a preface before it. Its place in the prayer is like the place of the *tawaf al-ziyarah* (the circumambulation of visitation), and what precedes it, the standing at 'Arafah and its associated rites, are preliminaries before it. Just as the servant is nearest to his Lord while prostrating, so too he is nearest to Him in the rites while circling the House. For this reason one of the Companions said to someone who addressed him about a worldly matter during his tawaf: "Do you say this while we are face to face with Allah in our tawaf?" For this reason, and Allah knows best, bowing was placed before prostration as a gradual transition from one thing to what is higher than it.

He prescribed for him the repetition of these actions and words, since they are the nourishment of the heart and soul, without which neither can subsist. So their repetition is like repeating eating until one is satisfied, and drinking until one is quenched. If the hungry man took a single morsel and then stopped eating, what would it avail him?

For this reason one of the early generations said: "The likeness of one who prays without settling in his prayer is like the hungry man, who when food is brought to him takes one or two morsels. What do they avail him?"

Moreover, in the repetition of every word or action of servitude and nearness, and in making the second a thanks for the first, there is the attaining of more of it, knowledge, attentiveness, strength of heart, expansion of the breast, and the removal of rust and filth from the heart. This is like washing a garment again and again. This is the wisdom of Allah, which has dazzled minds in His creation and His command, and which points to the perfection of His mercy and kindness.

When he has completed his prayer and perfected it, and nothing remains but to depart from it, he is prescribed to sit before his Lord, praising Him with the best greetings, which are fit only for Him and not for anyone else.

Since it is the custom of kings to be greeted with various kinds of greetings, of actions and words that express submission, praise, and the request for permanence and enduring sovereignty, some are greeted with prostration, some with praise of them, some with a request for their continuance and permanence, and some are given all of these together. The true King, glorified is He, is more deserving of all greetings than all of His creation, and they belong to Him in truth. For this reason *al-tahiyyat* has been explained as "sovereignty," and it has been explained as "permanence and everlastingness," and its reality is what I have mentioned, namely the greetings of kingship. The true, manifest King is most deserving of them.

So every greeting with which a king is greeted, whether by prostration, praise, or permanence and everlastingness, belongs to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. For this reason it is expressed in the plural and definite with the *alif-lam* as the particle of generality. It is the plural of *tahiyyah*, which is from *al-hayah* (life), and its original form is *tahiyyah* on the pattern of *takrimah*, then one of the two identical letters was assimilated into the other, becoming *tahiyyah*. Since its origin is from life, what is sought for the one greeted with it is the continuance of life.

They used to say to their kings: "To you be the enduring life, to you be the everlasting life," and some would say, "Ten thousand years," and from this they derived: "May Allah make your days endure, and prolong your survival," and similar expressions meaning the continuance of life and kingship. This is not fitting except for the Living who does not die, and for the King whose every kingdom is perishable apart from His kingdom.

Then He joined to it "*al-salawat*" (the prayers) in the plural and definite form, so as to include everything to which the word prayer has been applied, specifically and generally. All of them belong to Allah and are fit only for Him. So the greetings are His as sovereignty, and the prayers are His as servitude and deserving. The greetings belong to none but Him, and the prayers are fit for none but Him.

Then He joined to them "*al-tayyibat*" (the good things) likewise, and this encompasses two matters: attribute and sovereignty.

As for attribute, He, glorified is He, is good (*tayyib*), His speech is good, all His actions are good, and nothing proceeds from Him but the good, nothing is ascribed to Him but the good, and nothing ascends to Him but the good. So the good things belong to Him by attribute, action, speech and ascription. Every good thing is ascribed to Him, and everything ascribed to Him is good. So to Him belong the good words and the good actions, and every thing ascribed to Him, such as His House, His servant, His spirit, His she-camel and His Paradise, is good.

Also, the meanings of the good words belong to Allah alone, for the good words include His glorification, praise, magnification, exaltation, and praise of Him for His blessings and attributes. These good words by which He is praised, and their meanings, belong to Him alone; no other shares in them with Him, such as "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You, blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You," and similar: "Glory be to Allah," "Praise be to Allah," "There is no god but Allah," "Allah is greatest," and similar: "Glory be to Allah and by His praise, Glory be to Allah the Mighty."

Every good thing is for Him, with Him, from Him and to Him. He is good and accepts only what is good, and He is the God of the good, and His neighbours in the abode of His honour are the good.

Consider the best words after the Qur'an, how they are fit only for Allah: "Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, Allah is greatest, and there is no power nor might except by Allah." "Glory be to Allah" includes His declaration of freedom from every deficiency, defect and evil, and from the characteristics and likenesses of created beings. "Praise be to Allah" includes affirming every perfection for Him, in word, action and attribute, in the most complete and perfect manner, eternally and everlastingly. "There is no god but Allah" includes His singularity in divinity, that every object of worship other than Him is false, that He alone is the true God, and that whoever takes another as a god is like one who builds for himself a house of spiders' webs in which to dwell. "Allah is greatest" includes that He is greater than everything, more majestic, more mighty, more powerful, more capable, more knowing and wiser. These good words, with their meanings, are fit for none but Allah alone.

Then He prescribed for him to give the salam to the chosen servants of Allah, after preceding it with praise and extolment of Him as He deserves. This corresponds to His saying: ﴿Say: "Praise be to Allah, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen"﴾ [al-Naml: 59], and it is as if it were compliance with it. Moreover, this is the greeting of the created, so it was legislated after the greeting of the Creator. In this greeting the most deserving of creation is mentioned first, namely the Prophet ﷺ, through whose hand his community attained every good, and then upon himself after him, and upon all the righteous servants of Allah. Among these, the prophets are especially singled out with this greeting, then the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, although it is general to every righteous servant of Allah in the earth and the heavens.

Then He prescribed for him, after the mention of this greeting and the salam upon whoever deserves salam, specifically and generally, to bear witness to the truth on which the prayer is built. This is one of its rights, and it does not benefit him except with its companion, which is the testimony that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. The prayer was concluded with it, as 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: "When you say that and have finished your prayer, if you wish to stand, then stand, and if you wish to sit, then sit."

This may be taken to mean the actual completion of the prayer, as the Kufans say, or the approach to its end and its nearing conclusion, as the people of the Hijaz and others say. In either case, the testimony of truth was made the conclusion of the prayer, just as it was prescribed to be the conclusion of life. Whoever's last words are "There is no god but Allah" enters Paradise. Likewise it was prescribed for one performing ablution to conclude his ablution with the two testimonies.

Then, when he has finished his prayer, he is permitted to ask for his need, and it was prescribed for him to seek a means before it through sending blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ, for it is among the greatest means before supplication. As in the Sunan, on the authority of Fadalah ibn 'Ubayd, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When one of you supplicates, let him begin with praising Allah and extolling Him, then let him send blessings upon His Messenger, and then let him ask for his need."

So the greetings came in accordance with this: first the praise of Allah and extolling Him, then the blessing upon His Messenger, then the supplication at the end of the prayer. The Prophet ﷺ permitted the one praying, after sending blessings upon him, to choose from among the supplications whichever he likes best. A parallel to this is what was prescribed for one who hears the muezzin: that he say as he says, and that he say: "I am pleased with Allah as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad ﷺ as Messenger," and that he ask Allah for the Messenger's *wasilah* (means of nearness) and *fadilah* (excellence), and that He raise him to the praised station, then that he send blessings upon him, and then ask for his need. These are five sunnahs in responding to the muezzin, which should not be neglected.

(Section)

The secret of prayer, its spirit and its essence, is the servant's turning toward God with his whole being. Just as he should not turn his face away from the qibla of God to the right or to the left, so too he should not turn his heart away from his Lord toward anything else. The Ka'bah, which is the House of God, is the qibla of his face and body, and the Lord of the House, blessed and exalted, is the qibla of his heart and spirit. In proportion to the servant's turning toward God in his prayer, God turns toward him; and if he turns away, God turns away from him.

Turning toward God in prayer has three stations. The first is turning toward his heart, guarding it against the whisperings and thoughts that nullify the reward of his prayer or diminish it. The second is turning toward God by being mindful of Him, until it is as if he sees Him. The third is turning toward the meanings of His speech and the details of the servitude of prayer, giving each its due. By completing these three stations the establishment of prayer becomes true, and God's turning toward His servant is according to this.

When the servant stands upright before Him, his turning is toward His self-subsistence (qayyumiyyah) and His greatness. When he says "Allahu akbar," his turning is toward His supremacy (kibriya'). When he glorifies Him and praises Him, his turning is toward the radiance (subuhat) of His face, His transcendence above what does not befit Him, and praise of Him with the attributes of His beauty. When he seeks refuge in Him, his turning is toward His mighty support, His victory for His servant, His protection of him and His guarding him from his enemy. When he recites His speech, his turning is toward knowing Him through His speech, until it is as if he sees Him and witnesses Him in His speech. Thus, as one of the early pious predecessors said: "God has manifested Himself to His servants in His speech." In this state he is turned toward His essence, His attributes, His actions, His rulings and His names.

When he bows, his turning is toward His greatness, His majesty and His might, and for this reason he is prescribed to say: "Subhana Rabbiya al-'Azim" (Glory be to my Lord, the Mighty). When he raises his head from bowing, his turning is toward His praise, extolling Him, glorifying Him, his servitude to Him, and His sole right to give and to withhold. When he prostrates, his turning is toward His nearness, drawing close to Him, humility before Him, abasement before Him, brokenness and supplication. When he raises his head and sits on his knees, his turning is toward His self-sufficiency, His generosity and His munificence, and the servant's intense need for Him, his humble entreaty before Him and his brokenness, that He forgive him, have mercy on him, grant him well-being, guide him and provide for him.

When he sits for the tashahhud, he has another state and another turning, resembling the state of the pilgrim in the farewell tawaf. His heart senses his departure from before his Lord and the return of the attachments and preoccupations which standing before Him had cut off. He has tasted the pain and torment of his heart because of them, and has experienced the comfort of nearness and the bliss of turning toward God and its consequence, and their cessation from him during the prayer. Then his heart senses their return to him as he exits the sanctuary of prayer. So he bears the concern of the prayer's ending and conclusion, and says: "Would that it had been joined to the Day of Meeting." He knows that he is departing from intimate conversation with the One in whose conversation is all happiness, to intimate conversation with the One in whose conversation there is harm, worry, grief and vexation. None feels this except a living heart, full of the remembrance of God, His love and intimacy with Him.

Since the servant stands between two commands from his Lord, mighty and majestic:

The first: a decree upon him in all his states, outwardly and inwardly, requiring him to perform the servitude due to that decree, for every decree has a servitude specific to it. I mean the cosmic, predestined decree.

The second: an act the servant performs as servitude to his Lord, which is the requirement of His legislative, religious command.

Both commands necessitate the surrender of the self to Him, the Exalted. For this reason the name Islam (submission) was derived for it from surrender (taslim). When he surrenders himself to the religious, commanding decree of his Lord and to His cosmic, predestined decree, by performing servitude within it rather than by yielding to what he desires, he merits the name Islam, and it is said of him: "Muslim." When his heart is at rest through His remembrance, His speech, His love and His servitude, he finds tranquility in Him, his eye is comforted by Him, and he attains security through his faith.

Thus the performance of these two commands is necessary for him; he has no life, no success and no happiness except through them.

Since the soul that commands evil (nafs ammarah), the inclining desire, the demanding natures and the misleading Satan with which he has been afflicted would require him to waste his share of this or diminish it, the mercy of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful, required that He legislate prayer for him, compensating him for what he lost, restoring what had gone, renewing what had decayed of his faith. Its form was made to resemble the form of his actions: humility, submission, obedience and surrender. He gave every limb its share of servitude. He made its fruit and spirit the servant's turning toward his Lord in it with his whole being, and made its reward and recompense nearness to Him and attaining His honor in this world and the next. He made its station and place entering into the presence of God, blessed and exalted, and adorning oneself for presentation before Him, as a reminder of the Greatest Presentation before Him on the Day of Meeting.

Just as the fruit of fasting is the purification of the soul, the fruit of zakat is the purification of wealth, the fruit of hajj is the obligation of forgiveness, and the fruit of jihad is the surrender of the self which He, glorified be He, purchased from the believers, making Paradise its price, so the fruit of prayer is turning toward God and God's turning toward the servant. In that turning is contained all that has been mentioned of the fruits of the deeds. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ did not say: "My eye's delight has been made in fasting, nor in hajj and 'umrah," but he said: "My eye's delight has been made in prayer."

Consider his words: "My eye's delight has been made in prayer," and he did not say "with prayer," indicating that his eye is comforted by entering into it, just as the eye of the lover is comforted by being in contact with his beloved, and the eye of the one who fears is comforted by entering the place of his safety. The comfort of the eye through entering a thing is more complete and perfect than the comfort of the eye by it before entering. When he came to the rest of the heart from its fatigue and weariness, he said: "O Bilal, give us rest by prayer" (arihna bil-salah), meaning: establish it so that we may rest through it from the toil of preoccupations, just as the weary traveller rests when he reaches his lodging, settles there and calms down.

Consider how he said "give us rest by it," and did not say "give us rest from it," as the one who performs it under compulsion and as a burden says. When his heart is filled with other things, and it comes cutting him off from his affairs and beloved things, and he knows that he must perform it, he is saying with the tongue of his state and his speech: "We pray and rest from the prayer," not "by it." This is one color, and that is another. The difference is between one for whom prayer is a fetter to his needs, a prison to his heart and an obstacle to his soul, and one for whom prayer is a delight to his heart, the comfort of his eye, the ease of his needs, and a garden and pleasure to his soul.

The first: prayer is a prison for his soul and a restraint to keep it from plunging into the places of destruction. Through it they may attain expiation and reward, and they receive mercy in proportion to their servitude to God in it. The other category: prayer is the garden of their hearts, the comfort of their eyes, the delight of their souls, and the meadows of their limbs; in it they move about in bliss. The prayer of these people necessitates nearness and rank with God. They share with the first group in their reward, but they are distinguished by its highest level and by increase in rank and nearness, which is an amount beyond mere reward. For this reason kings promise those who please them with wages and proximity, as the sorcerers said to Pharaoh: "Shall we indeed have a reward if we are the victors?" He said: "Yes, and indeed you will then be among those brought near" (al-Shu'ara' 41–42).

The first is a servant who has entered the house while the veil stands between him and the Lord of the House, so he is behind the veil; therefore his eye is not comforted, because he is in the veils of desires, the clouds of passion, the smoke of the soul, and the vapor of wishes. The heart is sick, and the soul is prostrate upon what it desires, seeking its immediate share. The other has entered the abode of the King, and the veil between him and Him has been lifted; so his eye is comforted, his soul is at rest, his heart and limbs are humbled, and he worships God as if he sees Him, and He manifests Himself to him in His speech.

This is a hint and a very brief sketch concerning the taste of prayer.

(Section)

How excellent is what Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi said in some of his admonitions: "Presence of the heart is the first station of prayer. When you descend to it, you move on to the desert of meaning. When you depart from it, you kneel at the door of intimate conversation. The first hospitality for the guest is wakefulness and the unveiling of the veil for the eye of the heart. How can one who has not gone out into the desert hope to enter Mecca? You send your heart into every valley, so prayer often surprises you while your heart is not with you; you send the messenger after it, but he does not find it, and you enter prayer without a heart. The point is that it is shameful for the servant to say with his tongue 'Allahu akbar' while his heart is filled with other than God. He is the qibla of his heart in prayer, yet perhaps he is not present before his Lord in any part of it. If he fulfilled the right of 'Allahu akbar' and came to the House by its door, he would enter and depart with all kinds of gifts and goods. This is the door through which the worshipper enters, which is the takbir (opening). As for the door through which he exits, it is the door of peace (salam), which contains one of the Beautiful Names, so that he begins his prayer with His name, blessed and exalted, and concludes it with His name; he remembers the name of his Lord at the beginning and end of the prayer. He enters it with His name and leaves it with His name, along with what the name al-Salam has of special quality and wisdom suited to the worshipper's departure from before God, exalted be He. For as long as the worshipper is in his prayer before his Lord, he is in His sanctuary, which no one can violate; he is in a sanctuary protected from all calamities and evils. When he departs from before Him, blessed and exalted, calamities, afflictions and trials rush upon him from every side, and Satan comes to him with his snares and his troops; he is exposed to all kinds of afflictions and trials. But when he departs from before God accompanied by peace, a guardian from God remains over him until the next prayer time, and it is part of the completion of blessing upon him that his departure from before his Lord be in peace, which he carries with him, which endures for him and remains with him."

Reflect upon this secret, which, even if this annotation contained nothing else, would be sufficient; how much more so when it contains secrets and benefits not found among the people of this age. And praise for that belongs to God alone.

(Section: Turning the Head in Prayer)

His words in the hadith: "He has commanded you to pray; when you pray, do not turn (yaltafitu), for God directs His face toward the face of His servant in his prayer as long as he does not turn." The turning forbidden in prayer is of two kinds. The first: the turning of the heart away from God, exalted be He, toward other than God. The second: the turning of the sight. Both are forbidden.

God does not cease to turn toward His servant as long as the servant turns toward his prayer. When he turns with his heart or his sight, God, exalted be He, turns away from him.

The Messenger of God ﷺ was asked about a man's turning in his prayer, and he said: "It is a snatching which Satan snatches from the prayer of the servant." In a report, God says: "Toward something better than Me? Toward something better than Me?"

The likeness of one who turns in his prayer with his sight or his heart is like a man whom the ruler has summoned, and who has been made to stand before him; he begins to address and speak to him, while in the midst of this he turns away from the ruler to the right and to the left, and his heart has departed from the ruler, so he does not understand what is said to him, because his heart is not present with him. What do you think this man expects the ruler to do with him? Is not the least of his rank that he is dismissed from before him, despised, far away, and fallen from his eyes?

This worshipper is not equal to one whose heart is present, turned toward God in his prayer, who has made his heart aware of the greatness of the One before whom he stands, so that his heart is filled with His awe, his neck is humbled before Him, and he is ashamed before his Lord to turn toward another or to turn away from Him.

Between their two prayers, as Hassan 'Atiyyah said: "Two men may be in the same prayer, and the difference between them in merit is like that between heaven and earth, for one of them is turned toward God, exalted be He, while the other is heedless and negligent."

When the servant turns toward a creature like himself with a veil between them, it is not turning toward him nor nearness; what then do you think of the Creator, exalted be He?
