For this reason what was sought for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is blessings like the blessings upon Ibrahim and upon all the prophets after him and the believing family. For this reason this blessing is the most complete and the most excellent with which one sends blessings upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ). When the worshipper has offered it, he is commanded to seek refuge in God from all forms of evil, for evil is either the punishment of the Hereafter or its cause. So evil is only the punishment and its causes. The punishment is of two kinds: punishment in the barzakh (the intermediate realm) and punishment in the Hereafter. Its causes are trials, which are of two kinds: the greater and the lesser. The greater trial is the trial of the Dajjal (Antichrist) and the trial of death. The lesser trial is the trial of life, which can be remedied by repentance, unlike the trial of death and the trial of the Dajjal, for the one afflicted by them cannot remedy them.

Then he is prescribed from among the supplications what he chooses concerning the benefits of his worldly life and his Hereafter. Supplication in this place before the salam is better than supplication after the salam, and more beneficial for the one who supplicates. Likewise, most of the supplications of the Prophet (ﷺ) were in the prayer from its beginning to its end. He used to supplicate in the opening supplication with various kinds of supplication, after the bowing, after raising his head from it, in prostration, between the two prostrations, and in the tashahhud before the salam. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may God be pleased with him) was taught a supplication to say in his prayer, and al-Hasan ibn Ali was taught a supplication to recite in the qunut (supplication) of the witr prayer.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 23, verses 1–2 (part 3 of 6):

It was his practice that when he supplicated for a people or against a people, he would do so in the prayer after the bowing (ruku'). Among this is that the one praying, before his salam, is in the place of intimate conversation and nearness before his Lord, so supplication in this state is closer to being answered than supplication after he has departed from before Him. The Prophet ﷺ was asked, "Which supplication is most likely to be heard?" and he said: "The middle of the night and the end of the obligatory prayers." The *dubur* (end, last part) of the prayer is its final portion, like the *dubur* of an animal or the back of a wall. The *dubur* of the prayer may also refer to what comes after its conclusion, when there is an indication that shows this, as in his saying: "Glorify Allah, praise Him, and magnify Him, *dubur* of every prayer, thirty-three times each." Here *dubur* means the completion of the prayer. This is similar to the expiry of a term (ajal): the term is said to have its last part and is also said to have reached its end and conclusion.

(Section)

Then the prayer is concluded with the salam, and it is made the *tahlil* (release, the act by which one exits the state of prayer), by which the one praying leaves it, just as one leaves the state of ihram of Hajj by the *tahlil* of Hajj. The imam's *tahlil* is a supplication by him for those behind him for safety (*salamah*), which is the root and foundation of all good. So it was prescribed for those behind him to make their *tahlil* in the same way as the imam made his, and in this there is a supplication for him and for those praying with him for peace. Then this was prescribed for every worshipper, even if he prays alone, for there is no better release from the prayer than this. Just as there is no better opening of it than the *takbir* as its *tahrim* (the act that makes it forbidden to do otherwise), so its *tahrim* is the magnifying of the Lord, Exalted is He, which combines affirming every perfection for Him, declaring Him free of every deficiency and defect, singling Him out and specifying Him with this, and exalting and glorifying Him. The *takbir* includes the details of the prayer's actions, words and forms, so the prayer from beginning to end is an elaboration of the content of "Allahu Akbar." What *tahrim* could be better than this *tahrim*, which contains sincerity (*ikhlas*) and monotheism (*tawhid*)? And this *tahlil* contains beneficence toward one's believing brothers. Thus it opens with sincerity and closes with beneficence.

He said in the book (*al-Kalam ʿala Masʾalat al-Sama'*):

Then He prescribed for them the raising of the hands at the bowing, as a glorification of Allah's command, an adornment of the prayer, and a special servitude of the hands like the servitude of the rest of the limbs, and as following the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. So it is the ornament of the prayer, its adornment, and a magnification of its rites.

Then He prescribed the *takbir*, which occurs in the transitions of the prayer from one pillar to another, like the *talbiyah* in the transitions of the pilgrim from one station (mash'ar) to another. So it is the emblem of the prayer, just as the talbiyah is the emblem of Hajj, so that the servant may know that the secret of the prayer is the magnifying of the Lord, Exalted is He, and glorifying Him by worshipping Him alone.

Then He prescribed for him to humble himself before the Worshipped, glorified is He, by bowing, in humility before His greatness, submission to His awe, and lowliness before His might. So the servant bends his spine for Him, sets his stature for Him, lowers his head for Him, and bows his back for Him, magnifying Him and speaking His glorification together with His magnification. Thus there gathers for him the humility of the heart, the humility of the limbs, and the humility of speech, in the most complete state. In this dhikr he combined humility and magnification toward his Lord, and the declaration of His freedom from the humility of servants, for humility is the attribute of the servant and greatness is the attribute of the Lord.

The perfection of the servitude of bowing is that the servant become small and diminished, such that his diminishing erases every magnification of himself, and establishes in its place the magnification of his Lord. Whenever the magnifying of the Lord takes hold of his heart, his own smallness in his own eyes increases. So bowing belongs primarily and intentionally to the heart, and to the limbs by way of consequence and completion.

Then He prescribed for him to praise his Lord and extol Him for His blessings when he rises and stands upright, returning to his best posture, erect and balanced in stature. He praises his Lord and extols Him for having enabled him to that humility, then moved him from it to the station of standing and balance before Him, standing in His service. Just as in the state of recitation, this standing has a special savour and a state that arises in the heart distinct from the savour and state of bowing. It is a pillar intended for its own sake, the same as the pillar of bowing and prostration. For this reason the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would prolong it as he prolonged bowing and prostration, and he would increase in it praise, glorification and exaltation, as we have mentioned in his guidance ﷺ. In night prayer he would repeat often, "To my Lord is the praise, to my Lord is the praise."

Then He prescribed for him to say the *takbir* and fall down prostrate. In his prostration he gives every limb its share of servitude. He places his forehead on the ground before his Lord, pressing it down, rubbing his nose in dust before Him, his heart humbled to Him. He places the noblest part of himself, which is his face, upon the ground, especially upon dust, rubbing it before his Master, rubbing his nose, his heart and limbs humbled to Him, submitting to His greatness, bowing to His might, humbled before Him. He is the most abased and most broken of things before his Lord, Exalted is He, glorifying Him for His exaltation within his utmost lowliness, his upper parts turned down to his lower parts in abasement, submission and brokenness. His heart has conformed to the state of his body, so the heart prostrates as the face prostrates. His nose, his hands, his knees and his feet prostrate with it. He prescribed that he lift his thighs from his shins, his belly from his thighs, and his elbows from his sides, so that every part of him takes its share of humility, and no part bears another. It is most fitting in this state that he be nearer to his Lord than in other states, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating." Since the prostration of the heart is its complete submission to its Lord, it is possible to continue this prostration until the day one meets Him. As it was said to one of the early generations: "Does the heart prostrate?" He said: "Yes, by Allah! A prostration from which he does not lift his head until he meets Allah."

Since the prayer was built on five: the recitation, the standing, the bowing, the prostration and the dhikr, it was named after each of these five. It was called *qiyam* (standing), as in His saying: ﴿Stand [in prayer] at night, except a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 2], and His saying: ﴿And stand before Allah devoutly obedient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238]. It was called *qira'ah* (recitation), as in His saying: ﴿And the recitation of dawn; indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed﴾ [al-Isra': 78]. It was called *ruku'* (bowing), as in His saying: ﴿And bow with those who bow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 43], and His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow," they do not bow﴾ [al-Mursalat: 48]. It was called *sujud* (prostration), as in His saying: ﴿So glorify with the praise of your Lord and be among those who prostrate﴾ [al-Hijr: 98], and His saying: ﴿No! Do not obey him, but prostrate and draw near﴾ [al-'Alaq: 19]. It was called *dhikr* (remembrance), as in His saying: ﴿When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday, then hasten to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 9], and His saying: ﴿Let not your wealth or your children divert you from the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 9]. The noblest of its actions is the prostration, and the noblest of its invocations is the recitation. The first surah revealed to the Prophet ﷺ began with recitation and ended with prostration, and the rak'ah was constructed upon this: its beginning is recitation and its end is prostration.

Then He prescribed for him to raise his head and sit upright. Since this sitting is enclosed between two prostrations, one before it and one after it, moving from prostration to it and then from it to prostration, it has its own significance.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ would prolong it to the length of the prostration, and in it he would plead humbly to his Lord and seek His forgiveness, asking Him for His mercy, guidance, provision and well-being. It has a special savour and a state of the heart distinct from the savour and state of prostration. In this sitting the servant has taken the form of one kneeling before his Lord, casting himself before Him, apologising to Him for what he has committed, desiring that He forgive him and have mercy on him, seeking aid against his own commanding soul (*nafs ammarah*). The Prophet ﷺ would repeat the seeking of forgiveness in this sitting and increase his longing for Allah in it.

So picture yourself as a debtor who owes the right of Allah, while you are the guarantor of it, and the debtor is evasive and deceitful. You are being pursued on the guarantee, and the debtor is being pursued for the right, so you seek aid against him until you extract what is owed from him to free yourself from the demand. The heart is the partner of the soul in good and evil, reward and punishment, praise and blame. The soul's nature is to flee and to leave the bondage of servitude and to squander the rights of Allah that are due. The heart is its partner, and if its authority grows strong, it becomes its captive, and it is the partner and captive of the soul if the soul's authority grows strong.

So He prescribed for the servant, when he raises his head from prostration, to kneel before Allah seeking aid against his own soul, apologising to his Lord for what it has done, desiring that He have mercy on him, forgive him, guide him, provide for him and grant him well-being. These five are the sum of the good of this world and the Hereafter, for the servant is in need, indeed compelled, to secure his benefits in this world and the Hereafter and to ward off harms from himself in this world and the Hereafter. This supplication includes them all: provision brings him the benefits of his worldly life, well-being repels its harms, guidance brings him the benefits of his next life, forgiveness repels its harms, and mercy encompasses all of that.

He prescribed for him to return to prostration as he was before, and not to suffice with a single prostration in the rak'ah as he sufficed with a single bowing, because of the excellence and nobility of prostration, its station with Allah, and that He is nearest to His servant while he is prostrating. It is more deeply rooted in servitude and more firmly established in it than anything else. For this reason it was made the conclusion of the rak'ah, and what precedes it is like a preface before it. Its place in the prayer is like the place of the *tawaf al-ziyarah* (the circumambulation of visitation), and what precedes it, the standing at 'Arafah and its associated rites, are preliminaries before it. Just as the servant is nearest to his Lord while prostrating, so too he is nearest to Him in the rites while circling the House. For this reason one of the Companions said to someone who addressed him about a worldly matter during his tawaf: "Do you say this while we are face to face with Allah in our tawaf?" For this reason, and Allah knows best, bowing was placed before prostration as a gradual transition from one thing to what is higher than it.

He prescribed for him the repetition of these actions and words, since they are the nourishment of the heart and soul, without which neither can subsist. So their repetition is like repeating eating until one is satisfied, and drinking until one is quenched. If the hungry man took a single morsel and then stopped eating, what would it avail him?

For this reason one of the early generations said: "The likeness of one who prays without settling in his prayer is like the hungry man, who when food is brought to him takes one or two morsels. What do they avail him?"

Moreover, in the repetition of every word or action of servitude and nearness, and in making the second a thanks for the first, there is the attaining of more of it, knowledge, attentiveness, strength of heart, expansion of the breast, and the removal of rust and filth from the heart. This is like washing a garment again and again. This is the wisdom of Allah, which has dazzled minds in His creation and His command, and which points to the perfection of His mercy and kindness.

When he has completed his prayer and perfected it, and nothing remains but to depart from it, he is prescribed to sit before his Lord, praising Him with the best greetings, which are fit only for Him and not for anyone else.

Since it is the custom of kings to be greeted with various kinds of greetings, of actions and words that express submission, praise, and the request for permanence and enduring sovereignty, some are greeted with prostration, some with praise of them, some with a request for their continuance and permanence, and some are given all of these together. The true King, glorified is He, is more deserving of all greetings than all of His creation, and they belong to Him in truth. For this reason *al-tahiyyat* has been explained as "sovereignty," and it has been explained as "permanence and everlastingness," and its reality is what I have mentioned, namely the greetings of kingship. The true, manifest King is most deserving of them.

So every greeting with which a king is greeted, whether by prostration, praise, or permanence and everlastingness, belongs to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. For this reason it is expressed in the plural and definite with the *alif-lam* as the particle of generality. It is the plural of *tahiyyah*, which is from *al-hayah* (life), and its original form is *tahiyyah* on the pattern of *takrimah*, then one of the two identical letters was assimilated into the other, becoming *tahiyyah*. Since its origin is from life, what is sought for the one greeted with it is the continuance of life.

They used to say to their kings: "To you be the enduring life, to you be the everlasting life," and some would say, "Ten thousand years," and from this they derived: "May Allah make your days endure, and prolong your survival," and similar expressions meaning the continuance of life and kingship. This is not fitting except for the Living who does not die, and for the King whose every kingdom is perishable apart from His kingdom.

Then He joined to it "*al-salawat*" (the prayers) in the plural and definite form, so as to include everything to which the word prayer has been applied, specifically and generally. All of them belong to Allah and are fit only for Him. So the greetings are His as sovereignty, and the prayers are His as servitude and deserving. The greetings belong to none but Him, and the prayers are fit for none but Him.

Then He joined to them "*al-tayyibat*" (the good things) likewise, and this encompasses two matters: attribute and sovereignty.

As for attribute, He, glorified is He, is good (*tayyib*), His speech is good, all His actions are good, and nothing proceeds from Him but the good, nothing is ascribed to Him but the good, and nothing ascends to Him but the good. So the good things belong to Him by attribute, action, speech and ascription. Every good thing is ascribed to Him, and everything ascribed to Him is good. So to Him belong the good words and the good actions, and every thing ascribed to Him, such as His House, His servant, His spirit, His she-camel and His Paradise, is good.

Also, the meanings of the good words belong to Allah alone, for the good words include His glorification, praise, magnification, exaltation, and praise of Him for His blessings and attributes. These good words by which He is praised, and their meanings, belong to Him alone; no other shares in them with Him, such as "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You, blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You," and similar: "Glory be to Allah," "Praise be to Allah," "There is no god but Allah," "Allah is greatest," and similar: "Glory be to Allah and by His praise, Glory be to Allah the Mighty."

Every good thing is for Him, with Him, from Him and to Him. He is good and accepts only what is good, and He is the God of the good, and His neighbours in the abode of His honour are the good.

Consider the best words after the Qur'an, how they are fit only for Allah: "Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, Allah is greatest, and there is no power nor might except by Allah." "Glory be to Allah" includes His declaration of freedom from every deficiency, defect and evil, and from the characteristics and likenesses of created beings. "Praise be to Allah" includes affirming every perfection for Him, in word, action and attribute, in the most complete and perfect manner, eternally and everlastingly. "There is no god but Allah" includes His singularity in divinity, that every object of worship other than Him is false, that He alone is the true God, and that whoever takes another as a god is like one who builds for himself a house of spiders' webs in which to dwell. "Allah is greatest" includes that He is greater than everything, more majestic, more mighty, more powerful, more capable, more knowing and wiser. These good words, with their meanings, are fit for none but Allah alone.

Then He prescribed for him to give the salam to the chosen servants of Allah, after preceding it with praise and extolment of Him as He deserves. This corresponds to His saying: ﴿Say: "Praise be to Allah, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen"﴾ [al-Naml: 59], and it is as if it were compliance with it. Moreover, this is the greeting of the created, so it was legislated after the greeting of the Creator. In this greeting the most deserving of creation is mentioned first, namely the Prophet ﷺ, through whose hand his community attained every good, and then upon himself after him, and upon all the righteous servants of Allah. Among these, the prophets are especially singled out with this greeting, then the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, although it is general to every righteous servant of Allah in the earth and the heavens.

Then He prescribed for him, after the mention of this greeting and the salam upon whoever deserves salam, specifically and generally, to bear witness to the truth on which the prayer is built. This is one of its rights, and it does not benefit him except with its companion, which is the testimony that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. The prayer was concluded with it, as 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: "When you say that and have finished your prayer, if you wish to stand, then stand, and if you wish to sit, then sit."

This may be taken to mean the actual completion of the prayer, as the Kufans say, or the approach to its end and its nearing conclusion, as the people of the Hijaz and others say. In either case, the testimony of truth was made the conclusion of the prayer, just as it was prescribed to be the conclusion of life. Whoever's last words are "There is no god but Allah" enters Paradise. Likewise it was prescribed for one performing ablution to conclude his ablution with the two testimonies.

Then, when he has finished his prayer, he is permitted to ask for his need, and it was prescribed for him to seek a means before it through sending blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ, for it is among the greatest means before supplication. As in the Sunan, on the authority of Fadalah ibn 'Ubayd, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When one of you supplicates, let him begin with praising Allah and extolling Him, then let him send blessings upon His Messenger, and then let him ask for his need."

So the greetings came in accordance with this: first the praise of Allah and extolling Him, then the blessing upon His Messenger, then the supplication at the end of the prayer. The Prophet ﷺ permitted the one praying, after sending blessings upon him, to choose from among the supplications whichever he likes best. A parallel to this is what was prescribed for one who hears the muezzin: that he say as he says, and that he say: "I am pleased with Allah as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad ﷺ as Messenger," and that he ask Allah for the Messenger's *wasilah* (means of nearness) and *fadilah* (excellence), and that He raise him to the praised station, then that he send blessings upon him, and then ask for his need. These are five sunnahs in responding to the muezzin, which should not be neglected.

(Section)

The secret of prayer, its spirit and its essence, is the servant's turning toward God with his whole being. Just as he should not turn his face away from the qibla of God to the right or to the left, so too he should not turn his heart away from his Lord toward anything else. The Ka'bah, which is the House of God, is the qibla of his face and body, and the Lord of the House, blessed and exalted, is the qibla of his heart and spirit. In proportion to the servant's turning toward God in his prayer, God turns toward him; and if he turns away, God turns away from him.

Turning toward God in prayer has three stations. The first is turning toward his heart, guarding it against the whisperings and thoughts that nullify the reward of his prayer or diminish it. The second is turning toward God by being mindful of Him, until it is as if he sees Him. The third is turning toward the meanings of His speech and the details of the servitude of prayer, giving each its due. By completing these three stations the establishment of prayer becomes true, and God's turning toward His servant is according to this.

When the servant stands upright before Him, his turning is toward His self-subsistence (qayyumiyyah) and His greatness. When he says "Allahu akbar," his turning is toward His supremacy (kibriya'). When he glorifies Him and praises Him, his turning is toward the radiance (subuhat) of His face, His transcendence above what does not befit Him, and praise of Him with the attributes of His beauty. When he seeks refuge in Him, his turning is toward His mighty support, His victory for His servant, His protection of him and His guarding him from his enemy. When he recites His speech, his turning is toward knowing Him through His speech, until it is as if he sees Him and witnesses Him in His speech. Thus, as one of the early pious predecessors said: "God has manifested Himself to His servants in His speech." In this state he is turned toward His essence, His attributes, His actions, His rulings and His names.

When he bows, his turning is toward His greatness, His majesty and His might, and for this reason he is prescribed to say: "Subhana Rabbiya al-'Azim" (Glory be to my Lord, the Mighty). When he raises his head from bowing, his turning is toward His praise, extolling Him, glorifying Him, his servitude to Him, and His sole right to give and to withhold. When he prostrates, his turning is toward His nearness, drawing close to Him, humility before Him, abasement before Him, brokenness and supplication. When he raises his head and sits on his knees, his turning is toward His self-sufficiency, His generosity and His munificence, and the servant's intense need for Him, his humble entreaty before Him and his brokenness, that He forgive him, have mercy on him, grant him well-being, guide him and provide for him.

When he sits for the tashahhud, he has another state and another turning, resembling the state of the pilgrim in the farewell tawaf. His heart senses his departure from before his Lord and the return of the attachments and preoccupations which standing before Him had cut off. He has tasted the pain and torment of his heart because of them, and has experienced the comfort of nearness and the bliss of turning toward God and its consequence, and their cessation from him during the prayer. Then his heart senses their return to him as he exits the sanctuary of prayer. So he bears the concern of the prayer's ending and conclusion, and says: "Would that it had been joined to the Day of Meeting." He knows that he is departing from intimate conversation with the One in whose conversation is all happiness, to intimate conversation with the One in whose conversation there is harm, worry, grief and vexation. None feels this except a living heart, full of the remembrance of God, His love and intimacy with Him.

Since the servant stands between two commands from his Lord, mighty and majestic:

The first: a decree upon him in all his states, outwardly and inwardly, requiring him to perform the servitude due to that decree, for every decree has a servitude specific to it. I mean the cosmic, predestined decree.

The second: an act the servant performs as servitude to his Lord, which is the requirement of His legislative, religious command.

Both commands necessitate the surrender of the self to Him, the Exalted. For this reason the name Islam (submission) was derived for it from surrender (taslim). When he surrenders himself to the religious, commanding decree of his Lord and to His cosmic, predestined decree, by performing servitude within it rather than by yielding to what he desires, he merits the name Islam, and it is said of him: "Muslim." When his heart is at rest through His remembrance, His speech, His love and His servitude, he finds tranquility in Him, his eye is comforted by Him, and he attains security through his faith.

Thus the performance of these two commands is necessary for him; he has no life, no success and no happiness except through them.

Since the soul that commands evil (nafs ammarah), the inclining desire, the demanding natures and the misleading Satan with which he has been afflicted would require him to waste his share of this or diminish it, the mercy of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful, required that He legislate prayer for him, compensating him for what he lost, restoring what had gone, renewing what had decayed of his faith. Its form was made to resemble the form of his actions: humility, submission, obedience and surrender. He gave every limb its share of servitude. He made its fruit and spirit the servant's turning toward his Lord in it with his whole being, and made its reward and recompense nearness to Him and attaining His honor in this world and the next. He made its station and place entering into the presence of God, blessed and exalted, and adorning oneself for presentation before Him, as a reminder of the Greatest Presentation before Him on the Day of Meeting.

Just as the fruit of fasting is the purification of the soul, the fruit of zakat is the purification of wealth, the fruit of hajj is the obligation of forgiveness, and the fruit of jihad is the surrender of the self which He, glorified be He, purchased from the believers, making Paradise its price, so the fruit of prayer is turning toward God and God's turning toward the servant. In that turning is contained all that has been mentioned of the fruits of the deeds. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ did not say: "My eye's delight has been made in fasting, nor in hajj and 'umrah," but he said: "My eye's delight has been made in prayer."

Consider his words: "My eye's delight has been made in prayer," and he did not say "with prayer," indicating that his eye is comforted by entering into it, just as the eye of the lover is comforted by being in contact with his beloved, and the eye of the one who fears is comforted by entering the place of his safety. The comfort of the eye through entering a thing is more complete and perfect than the comfort of the eye by it before entering. When he came to the rest of the heart from its fatigue and weariness, he said: "O Bilal, give us rest by prayer" (arihna bil-salah), meaning: establish it so that we may rest through it from the toil of preoccupations, just as the weary traveller rests when he reaches his lodging, settles there and calms down.

Consider how he said "give us rest by it," and did not say "give us rest from it," as the one who performs it under compulsion and as a burden says. When his heart is filled with other things, and it comes cutting him off from his affairs and beloved things, and he knows that he must perform it, he is saying with the tongue of his state and his speech: "We pray and rest from the prayer," not "by it." This is one color, and that is another. The difference is between one for whom prayer is a fetter to his needs, a prison to his heart and an obstacle to his soul, and one for whom prayer is a delight to his heart, the comfort of his eye, the ease of his needs, and a garden and pleasure to his soul.

The first: prayer is a prison for his soul and a restraint to keep it from plunging into the places of destruction. Through it they may attain expiation and reward, and they receive mercy in proportion to their servitude to God in it. The other category: prayer is the garden of their hearts, the comfort of their eyes, the delight of their souls, and the meadows of their limbs; in it they move about in bliss. The prayer of these people necessitates nearness and rank with God. They share with the first group in their reward, but they are distinguished by its highest level and by increase in rank and nearness, which is an amount beyond mere reward. For this reason kings promise those who please them with wages and proximity, as the sorcerers said to Pharaoh: "Shall we indeed have a reward if we are the victors?" He said: "Yes, and indeed you will then be among those brought near" (al-Shu'ara' 41–42).

The first is a servant who has entered the house while the veil stands between him and the Lord of the House, so he is behind the veil; therefore his eye is not comforted, because he is in the veils of desires, the clouds of passion, the smoke of the soul, and the vapor of wishes. The heart is sick, and the soul is prostrate upon what it desires, seeking its immediate share. The other has entered the abode of the King, and the veil between him and Him has been lifted; so his eye is comforted, his soul is at rest, his heart and limbs are humbled, and he worships God as if he sees Him, and He manifests Himself to him in His speech.

This is a hint and a very brief sketch concerning the taste of prayer.

(Section)

How excellent is what Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi said in some of his admonitions: "Presence of the heart is the first station of prayer. When you descend to it, you move on to the desert of meaning. When you depart from it, you kneel at the door of intimate conversation. The first hospitality for the guest is wakefulness and the unveiling of the veil for the eye of the heart. How can one who has not gone out into the desert hope to enter Mecca? You send your heart into every valley, so prayer often surprises you while your heart is not with you; you send the messenger after it, but he does not find it, and you enter prayer without a heart. The point is that it is shameful for the servant to say with his tongue 'Allahu akbar' while his heart is filled with other than God. He is the qibla of his heart in prayer, yet perhaps he is not present before his Lord in any part of it. If he fulfilled the right of 'Allahu akbar' and came to the House by its door, he would enter and depart with all kinds of gifts and goods. This is the door through which the worshipper enters, which is the takbir (opening). As for the door through which he exits, it is the door of peace (salam), which contains one of the Beautiful Names, so that he begins his prayer with His name, blessed and exalted, and concludes it with His name; he remembers the name of his Lord at the beginning and end of the prayer. He enters it with His name and leaves it with His name, along with what the name al-Salam has of special quality and wisdom suited to the worshipper's departure from before God, exalted be He. For as long as the worshipper is in his prayer before his Lord, he is in His sanctuary, which no one can violate; he is in a sanctuary protected from all calamities and evils. When he departs from before Him, blessed and exalted, calamities, afflictions and trials rush upon him from every side, and Satan comes to him with his snares and his troops; he is exposed to all kinds of afflictions and trials. But when he departs from before God accompanied by peace, a guardian from God remains over him until the next prayer time, and it is part of the completion of blessing upon him that his departure from before his Lord be in peace, which he carries with him, which endures for him and remains with him."

Reflect upon this secret, which, even if this annotation contained nothing else, would be sufficient; how much more so when it contains secrets and benefits not found among the people of this age. And praise for that belongs to God alone.

(Section: Turning the Head in Prayer)

His words in the hadith: "He has commanded you to pray; when you pray, do not turn (yaltafitu), for God directs His face toward the face of His servant in his prayer as long as he does not turn." The turning forbidden in prayer is of two kinds. The first: the turning of the heart away from God, exalted be He, toward other than God. The second: the turning of the sight. Both are forbidden.

God does not cease to turn toward His servant as long as the servant turns toward his prayer. When he turns with his heart or his sight, God, exalted be He, turns away from him.

The Messenger of God ﷺ was asked about a man's turning in his prayer, and he said: "It is a snatching which Satan snatches from the prayer of the servant." In a report, God says: "Toward something better than Me? Toward something better than Me?"

The likeness of one who turns in his prayer with his sight or his heart is like a man whom the ruler has summoned, and who has been made to stand before him; he begins to address and speak to him, while in the midst of this he turns away from the ruler to the right and to the left, and his heart has departed from the ruler, so he does not understand what is said to him, because his heart is not present with him. What do you think this man expects the ruler to do with him? Is not the least of his rank that he is dismissed from before him, despised, far away, and fallen from his eyes?

This worshipper is not equal to one whose heart is present, turned toward God in his prayer, who has made his heart aware of the greatness of the One before whom he stands, so that his heart is filled with His awe, his neck is humbled before Him, and he is ashamed before his Lord to turn toward another or to turn away from Him.

Between their two prayers, as Hassan 'Atiyyah said: "Two men may be in the same prayer, and the difference between them in merit is like that between heaven and earth, for one of them is turned toward God, exalted be He, while the other is heedless and negligent."

When the servant turns toward a creature like himself with a veil between them, it is not turning toward him nor nearness; what then do you think of the Creator, exalted be He? And when he turns toward the Creator, exalted be He, while between him and Him is the veil of desires, whisperings, and a soul enamored of them and filled with them, how can that be turning, when whisperings and thoughts have distracted him and carried him off in every direction? When the servant stands in prayer, Satan is jealous of him, for he has stood in the greatest and nearest station, the most vexing to Satan and the most grievous to him. So Satan strives and works hard that he not stand in it; he never ceases to promise him, wish for him, make him forget, and bring against him his cavalry and infantry, until the matter of prayer becomes light in his eyes, and he neglects it, and abandons it.

If Satan fails in this, and the servant disobeys him and stands in that station, the enemy of God approaches until he suggests thoughts between him and himself, and comes between him and his heart. He reminds him during prayer of things he did not remember before entering it, until perhaps he has forgotten something and despaired of it, and then he reminds him of it during prayer, to occupy his heart with it and seize him from God, exalted be He, so that he stands in prayer without a heart. He does not attain the turning of God, His honor and His nearness that the one who turns toward his Lord, exalted be He, and whose heart is present in his prayer, attains. So he departs from his prayer as he entered it, with his sins, his offenses and his burdens not lightened by the prayer. For prayer only expiates the evil deeds of one who fulfils its right, perfects its humility, and stands before God, exalted be He, with his heart and faces Him.

When such a person departs from it, he finds lightness in himself and feels that burdens have been lifted from him. He finds energy, comfort and spirit, so that he wishes he had not left it, because it is the comfort of his eyes, the bliss of his spirit, the paradise of his heart and his resting place in this world. He is always as if in a prison and constriction until he enters it, and rests by it, not from it.

The lovers say: "We pray and are rested by our prayer," as their leader, exemplar and prophet ﷺ said: "O Bilal, give us rest by prayer," and he did not say "give us rest from it." And he ﷺ said: "My eye's delight has been made in prayer." So how can the eye of one whose delight is in prayer be comforted without it, and how can he bear to be without it? The prayer of this one who is present in heart, whose eye's delight is in prayer, is the prayer that ascends with light and proof, until he meets the Most Merciful, exalted be He, and it says: "May God preserve you as you preserved me." As for the prayer of the negligent one who wastes its rights, its limits and its humility, it is wrapped up like a worn-out garment and struck against the face of its owner, and says: "May God waste you as you wasted me."

A marfu' hadith has been transmitted, related by Bakr ibn Bishr from Sa'id ibn Sinan from Abu al-Zahiriyyah from Abu Shajarah from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, may God be pleased with them both, traced to the Prophet, that he said: "No believer completes his ablution to its places, then stands for prayer at its time and performs it for God, exalted be He, without diminishing its time, its bowing, its prostration or its markers in anything, except that it is raised before God, exalted be He, bright and radiant, illuminating by its light what is between the two horizons until it reaches the Most Merciful, exalted be He. And whoever stands to prayer without perfecting its ablution, delays it beyond its time, and steals its bowing, its prostration and its markers, it is raised from him black and dark, and it does not pass beyond the hair of his head, saying: 'May God waste you as you wasted me, waste you as you wasted me.'"

So the accepted prayer and the accepted deed is that the servant prays a prayer befitting his Lord, exalted be He. When the prayer is fit for his Lord, blessed and exalted, and befitting Him, it is accepted.

(Section)

Know that complete delight, joy, happiness, pleasant living and bliss lie only in knowing God and His unity, intimacy with Him, longing for His meeting, and the gathering of the heart and its concern upon Him. For the most wretched life is that of one whose heart is scattered and whose concern is divided; he has no settled place for his heart, no beloved to which it may return and in which it may rest. As the poet expressed this in his saying:

"He who has no beloved to whom he may turn in peace and rest has never tasted the flavor of life."

The good life, the beneficial living and the coolness of the eye lie in the stillness and tranquility of the heart in the first Beloved. Even if the heart were to roam among all beloved things, it would not settle or find peace in any of them, nor would the eye be comforted by them, until it finds peace in its God, its Lord and its Friend, besides whom it has no friend or intercessor, and from whom it is not independent for the blink of an eye. As the poet said:

"Shift your heart wherever you wish of desires; love is only for the first Beloved."

"How many dwellings on earth does the youth grow fond of, yet his longing is always for the first dwelling."

So strive that your concern be one, and that it be He alone. This is the ultimate happiness of the servant. The possessor of this state is in a garden hastened before the Garden of the Hereafter, and in a bliss given in advance, as one of those who have found (al-wajidin) said: "There pass over the heart moments of which I say: if the people of Paradise are in the like of this, they are truly in a good life."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 23, verses 1–2 (part 5 of 6):

Another said: "There are times when the heart passes through a state in which it dances with delight." Another said: "The poor people of this world left it without tasting the best of what is in it..." It was said to him: "And what is the best of what is in it?" He said: "Knowing Allah, loving Him, finding intimacy in His nearness, and longing to meet Him. There is no bliss in this world that resembles the bliss of the people of Paradise except this. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Women and perfume have been made beloved to me from your world, and the coolness of my eyes has been placed in prayer.' He informed that two things were made beloved to him from the world: women and perfume. Then he said: 'and the coolness of my eyes has been placed in prayer.'"

The coolness of the eye (qurrat al-ayn) is above love (mahabba), for not every beloved is something in which the eye finds coolness. The eye is only cooled by the highest of beloved things, which is loved for its own sake, and that is none other than Allah, there is no god but Him. Everything else is loved only as a consequence of loving Him, so it is loved for His sake and is not loved alongside Him. Love alongside Him is shirk (associating partners with Allah), while love for His sake is tawhid (affirming Allah's oneness). The polytheist takes rivals besides Allah and loves them as he loves Allah, whereas the monotheist (muwahhid) loves whoever Allah loves, hates whoever Allah hates for Allah's sake, does what Allah does, and abandons what Allah abandons, for Allah's sake. The foundation of the religion rests on these four principles, which are love and hatred, and from them follow action and abstention, giving and withholding. Whoever perfects all of this for Allah has perfected faith, and whatever falls short of being for Allah, the faith of the servant decreases accordingly.

The point is that what the eye finds cool is higher than what is merely loved. Prayer is the coolness of the eyes of lovers in this world, because in it one converses with the One whom eyes cannot satisfy, hearts cannot be content with, and souls cannot rest with except by Him, and it is a delight in remembering Him, humbling oneself before Him, and drawing near to Him. This is especially so in prostration, and that state is when the servant is closest to his Lord. From this is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "O Bilal, give us rest by the prayer." Thereby you know that his (ﷺ) rest was in prayer, just as he informed that the coolness of his eye was in it. How far is this from the saying of one who says: "We pray and rest from the prayer!"

The lover finds his rest and the coolness of his eye in prayer, whereas the heedless and averse person has no share of this. Rather, prayer is a heavy and burdensome thing for him. When he stands in it, he is as if on hot coals, wanting to be free of it, and the most beloved prayer to him is the quickest and shortest, for he has no coolness of the eye in it and his heart finds no rest in it. When a servant's eye is cooled by something and his heart finds rest in it, the hardest thing for him is to be separated from it. The one who is artificial, empty of heart toward Allah and the Hereafter, and afflicted with love of this world, finds prayer the hardest, and the most hateful to him is its length, even though he is free, healthy, and unoccupied.

It should be known that the prayer in which the eye is cooled and the heart finds rest is the one that comprises six aspects (mashhad, pl. mashahid).

The first aspect is sincerity (ikhlas), which is that what moves him to it and calls him to it is the servant's desire for Allah, his love for Him, the seeking of His pleasure, nearness to Him, drawing close to Him in affection, and obeying His command, such that nothing of worldly portions at all motivates him to it. Rather, he performs it seeking the face of his Lord, the Most High, out of love for Him, fear of His punishment, and hope for His forgiveness and reward.

The second aspect is the aspect of truthfulness and sincere counsel (sidq wa nusḥ), which is that he empties his heart for Allah in it, exerts his utmost effort in turning to Allah in it, gathers his heart upon it, and performs it in the best and most complete manner, outwardly and inwardly. For prayer has an outward and an inward dimension. Its outward dimension is the visible actions and the audible words, and its inward dimension is humility (khushu'), vigilance (muraqaba), emptying the heart for Allah, and turning wholly to Allah in it, such that the heart does not turn away from Him to anything else. This inward dimension is like the spirit for it, while the actions are like the body. When it is devoid of spirit, it is like a body without a soul. Should the servant not be ashamed to confront his master with such a thing? For this reason it is rolled up as a worn-out garment is rolled up, and it is struck against the face of its owner, and it says: "May Allah lose you as you lost me."

The prayer whose outward and inward dimensions are both perfected ascends, having a light and a proof like the light of the sun, until it is presented to Allah, who is pleased with it and accepts it, and it says: "May Allah protect you as you protected me."

(Section)

The third aspect is the aspect of following and emulation (mutaba'a wa iqtida'), which is that he takes the utmost care to emulate the Prophet (ﷺ) in his prayer, praying as he used to pray, and turning away from what people have introduced into prayer of addition, omission, and forms from which nothing has been transmitted from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), nor from any of his Companions. He should not stop at the opinions of those who grant concessions, who stop at the least of what they believe to be obligatory, while others dispute them on this and consider obligatory what they have dropped. Perhaps the established hadiths and the Prophetic Sunnah are on the side of the others, yet they do not pay attention to that and say: "We are followers (muqallidun) of such-and-such a school." This does not benefit one before Allah, nor is it an excuse for one who neglects the Sunnah that has reached him. For Allah, glory be to Him, commanded only obedience to His Messenger and following him alone, and did not command following anyone else. Others are obeyed only when they command what the Messenger commanded. Every person other than the Messenger (ﷺ) is taken from his words and left.

Allah, glory be to Him, has sworn by His noble Self: "No, by your Lord, they do not believe until they make you judge in what they dispute among themselves, and then find within themselves no discomfort at what you decide, and submit fully." So judgment by anyone else, and submission to him, will not benefit us, nor will it save us from Allah's punishment, nor will this answer be accepted from us when we hear His call on the Day of Resurrection: "What did you answer the messengers?" For He will certainly question us about that and demand an answer. Allah, the Exalted, said: "We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It has been revealed to me that you will be tested in my name and questioned about me," meaning the questioning in the grave. Whoever has reached the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and abandons it for the saying of any person will be brought back on the Day of Resurrection and will know.

(Section)

The fourth aspect is the aspect of excellence (ihsan), which is the aspect of vigilance (muraqaba), that he worships Allah as if he sees Him. This aspect arises only from the perfection of faith in Allah, His names, and His attributes, until it is as if he sees Allah, glory be to Him, above His heavens, established upon His Throne, speaking with His command and prohibition, and managing the affairs of creation. Commands descend from Him and ascend to Him, and the deeds and spirits of the servants are presented to Him at the time of their return. He witnesses all of this with his heart, witnesses His names and attributes, and witnesses the Self-Subsisting, Living, All-Hearing, All-Seeing, Mighty, Wise, the Commander and Forbidder, who loves, hates, is pleased, is angered, does what He wills, and judges what He desires, and He is above His Throne. Nothing of the deeds of the servants, nor their words, nor their inner thoughts, is hidden from Him. Rather, He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the chests conceal.

The aspect of excellence is the root of all actions of the heart, for it necessitates modesty, reverence, glorification, awe, love, turning in repentance, reliance, humility before Allah, and submission to Him.

It cuts off whisperings and the discourse of the self,
and gathers the heart and its concerns upon Allah.

So the servant's share of nearness to Allah is according to his share of the station of excellence, and prayers differ accordingly, such that between the prayers of two men there is as much difference in merit as between the heaven and the earth, though their standing, bowing, and prostration are the same.

(Section)

The fifth aspect is the aspect of favor (minna), which is that he witnesses that favor belongs to Allah, glory be to Him, in that He placed him in this station, qualified him for it, and enabled him to stand with his heart and body in His service. Had it not been for Allah, none of that would have occurred. Just as the Companions used to sing before the Prophet (ﷺ), saying:

"By Allah, had it not been for Allah, we would not have been guided,
nor would we have given charity, nor would we have prayed."

Allah, the Exalted, said: "They count it as a favor to you that they have embraced Islam. Say: Do not count your Islam as a favor to me; rather, Allah has conferred a favor upon you that He guided you to faith, if you are truthful."

So Allah, glory be to Him, is the One who made the Muslim a Muslim and the one who prays one who prays, just as the Friend (Khalil) (ﷺ) said: "Our Lord, make us submitters to You, and from our offspring a Muslim community submitting to You." And he said: "My Lord, make me one who establishes prayer, and from my offspring."

So the favor belongs to Allah alone, in that He made His servant stand in obedience to Him, and this is among the greatest of His blessings upon him.

Allah, the Exalted, said: "Whatever blessing you have is from Allah." And He said: "But Allah has made faith beloved to you and beautified it in your hearts, and made disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience hateful to you. Those are the rightly guided."

This aspect is among the greatest and most beneficial of aspects for the servant, and the more the servant is perfect in tawhid, the greater his share of this aspect. In it is the benefit that it prevents the heart from self-admiration (ujb) for deeds and from seeing them, for when he witnesses that Allah, glory be to Him, is the Giver of it, the One who enables him and guides him to it, witnessing this occupies him from seeing himself and admiring it, and from displaying it against people. So he does not admire it in his heart, nor boast of it with his tongue, nor consider it great. This is the character of an elevated deed. Among its benefits is that it attributes praise to its Guardian and rightful owner, so he does not witness praise for himself, but witnesses all of it as belonging to Allah, just as he witnesses that all blessings are from Him, all favor is His, and all good is in His hands. This is among the perfections of tawhid, and his foot does not settle in the station of tawhid except by knowing this and witnessing it. When he knows it and it becomes firmly established in him, it becomes a station (mashhad) for him. When it becomes a station for his heart, it yields love, intimacy with Allah, longing to meet Him, and delight in remembering Him and obeying Him, of a kind with no comparison at all to the highest delights of this world.

What good is there for a man in his life if his heart is barred from this and the path to reaching it is blocked from him? Rather, it is as Allah, the Exalted, said: "Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them; they will soon know."

(Section)

The sixth aspect is the aspect of shortcoming (taqsir), which is that even if the servant strives to the utmost in fulfilling the command and expends his full effort, he is still deficient, and Allah's right over him is greater. What he ought to offer Him in obedience, servitude, and service should exceed that by much, and His greatness and majesty, glory be to Him, require the servitude that befits them.

If the servants of kings treat them in their service with honor, glorification, respect, reverence, modesty, awe, fear, and sincere counsel, so that they empty their hearts and limbs for them, then the Master of kings and the Lord of the heavens and the earth is more deserving of being treated in that way, indeed by multiples of it.

When the servant witnesses in himself that he has not fulfilled his Lord's right in servitude, nor even close to it, he knows his shortcoming, and despite that he has nothing but to seek forgiveness and to offer excuse for his shortcoming, his neglect, and his failure to perform what is due to Him of His right. He is in greater need, until Allah forgives him his servitude and pardons him in it, than he is in need of seeking a reward from Him for it. Even if he had fulfilled it as it ought to be fulfilled, it would still be owed to Him by the necessity of servitude. For the work and service of a servant to his master is owed to the master by virtue of his being his servant and slave. If he asked his master for a wage for his work and service, people would count him foolish and clumsy.

Yet he is not truly His servant or slave in reality, rather he is truly the servant and slave of Allah in every respect, to Allah, glory be to Him. So his work and service are owed to Allah by virtue of his being His servant. When He rewards him for it, that is pure bounty, favor, and kindness toward him, which the servant does not deserve from Him.

From here the meaning of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying is understood: "None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy and favor."

Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "On the Day of Resurrection three registers will be brought out for the servant: a register in which are his good deeds, a register in which are his evil deeds, and a register of the blessings with which Allah blessed him. The Lord, the Exalted, will say to His blessings: 'Take your right from the good deeds of My servant.' So the smallest of them will rise and exhaust his good deeds. Then they will say: 'By Your might, I have not yet received my full right.' When Allah wishes to show mercy to His servant, He gives him back his blessings, forgives his evil deeds, and multiplies his good deeds."

This is authentic from Anas, and it is the strongest evidence of the perfection of the Companions' knowledge of their Lord and of His rights over them, just as they were the most knowledgeable of the Ummah about their Prophet, his Sunnah, and his religion. In this report there is knowledge and recognition that none can grasp except those of insight who know Allah, His names, His attributes, and His rights.

From here is understood the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying in the hadith narrated by Abu Dawud and Imam Ahmad from the hadith of Zayd ibn Thabit, Hudhayfa, and others: "If Allah were to punish the people of His heavens and the people of His earth, He would punish them, and He would not be unjust to them. And if He were to show them mercy, His mercy would be better for them than their deeds."

(Section)

The essence of this matter rests on four things:
a sound intention, and a high resolve accompanied by hope and fear.

These four are the foundations of this matter, and whatever deficiency enters the servant's faith, states, outward conduct, or inward state, it stems from a deficiency in these four or a deficiency in some of them.

Let the intelligent person reflect on these four things, make them his path and conduct, and build upon them his knowledge, deeds, words, and states. Nothing emerges except from them, and no one falls short except by lacking them.

And Allah knows best, and Allah is the One sought for help, in whom is reliance, to whom is turning, and He is the One asked to grant us success, along with all our brothers from the People of the Sunnah, in realizing them in knowledge and action. He is the Protector of that and the Giver of it, and He is sufficient for us and the best Disposer of affairs.

(Section)

Accepted deeds are of two kinds.

(The first) is that the servant prays and performs all other acts of obedience while his heart is attached to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and remembers Allah constantly. The deeds of this servant are presented to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, until they stand before Him, and Allah looks at them. When He looks at them, He sees them as sincere for His face, pleasing, having issued from a sound, sincere heart that loves Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and draws near to Him. He loves them, is pleased with them, and accepts them.

(The second kind): the servant performs deeds out of habit and heedlessness, intending by them obedience and drawing near to Allah. His limbs are occupied with obedience, but his heart is distracted from the remembrance of Allah, and likewise all his other deeds. When the deeds of this person are raised to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, they do not stand before Him, nor does His gaze fall upon them. Rather, they are placed where the registers of deeds are placed, until they are presented to Him on the Day of Resurrection, and they are distinguished. He rewards him for what was done for Him among them, and returns to him what was not done for His face.

So His acceptance of this deed means rewarding him for it with one of His creations: palaces, food, drink, and the wide-eyed maidens. The reward of the first kind is His pleasure with the deed for its own sake, His pleasure with the one who performed it, His drawing him near, and the elevation of his rank and station. This one He gives without reckoning. So this is one kind, and the first is another kind.

(Section)

Now as for the prayer (al-salah), its concern is in gladdening and strengthening the heart, expanding it, bringing it joy and delight, which is the greatest concern. In it there is the connection of the heart and spirit with God, nearness to Him, savouring the remembrance of Him, rejoicing in intimate conversation with Him, standing before Him, and employing the whole body, its powers and its instruments, in His worship, giving every limb its share of it, and his being occupied away from attachment to creatures and their associations and conversations, and the drawing of the faculties of his heart and limbs toward his Lord and Originator, and his relief from his enemy during the prayer. Thus it becomes among the greatest of remedies, gladdeners and nourishments, which suit only healthy hearts.

As for sick hearts, they are like sick bodies, which are suited only by excellent foods.

So prayer is among the greatest aids to attaining the benefits of this world and the Hereafter and to warding off the harms of this world and the Hereafter. It forbids sin, repels the diseases of the hearts, drives away illness from the body, illuminates the heart, whitens the face, invigorates the limbs and the soul, brings sustenance, repels oppression, supports the oppressed, suppresses the rebellious impulses of desire, preserves blessings, averts calamities, brings down mercy, removes distress, and benefits many pains of the stomach.

Ibn Majah related in his Sunan, from the hadith of Mujahid, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw me while I was lying down complaining of a pain in my stomach, and he said to me: 'O Abu Hurayrah, has dard (colic) seized your stomach?'" He said: "I said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah.'" He said: "'Stand up and pray, for in prayer there is healing.'"

This hadith has also been narrated as a statement (mawquf) of Abu Hurayrah, and that he was the one who said that to Mujahid, and this is more likely. The meaning of this word in Persian is: "Does your stomach hurt you?"

If the chest of the zindiq (heretical) physicians is not opened to this remedy, let them be addressed in the language of medicine, and told: prayer is an exercise of the soul and body together, since it includes movements and various postures: standing, bowing, prostration, sitting in the tawarruk position, transitions, and others, of the postures in which most of the joints move and most of the inner organs, such as the stomach, the intestines and the rest of the instruments of digestion and nourishment, are gently pressed. Who can deny that in these movements there is strengthening and dissolution of the humours, especially through the strength of the soul and its expansion in prayer, so that the natural faculty is strengthened and pain is thereby repelled? But the disease of heresy, of turning away from what the messengers brought, and of substituting for it atheism, is a disease for which there is no cure, except a fire that blazes, which none will enter except the most wretched, who denied and turned away.

(Section)

If it is said: What do you say about a prayer performed without khushu' (humble attentiveness)? Is it counted or not?

It is said: As for being counted for reward, no reward is credited for it except for what of it the person understood and in which he humbled himself before his Lord.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "You have from your prayer only what you understood of it."

In the Musnad, it is related as a marfu' hadith: "Indeed the servant prays a prayer, and there is written for him only half of it, or a third of it, or a quarter of it, until it reaches a tenth of it."

Allah has tied the success (falah) of those who pray to their humility (khushu') in their prayer, which shows that whoever does not humble himself is not among the people of success, and if it were counted for him as reward he would be among the successful.

As for being counted in the rulings of this world, and the dropping of the obligation to make it up (qada'), if khushu' and understanding predominate in it, it is counted by consensus, and the sunan and the adhkar after it serve as compensations and completions for its deficiency.

If the lack of khushu' and understanding predominates in it, then the jurists have differed concerning the obligation of repeating it. Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Hamid of the companions of Ahmad, and Abu Hamid al-Ghazali in his Ihya' (but not in his Wasit or Basit), required its repetition.

They argued that it is a prayer for which one is not rewarded, and for which success was not guaranteed, so his obligation is not discharged by it, and the obligation to make it up does not fall from him, like the prayer of the show-off (al-mura'i).

They said: Also, because humility and understanding are the spirit of the prayer, its purpose and its essence. How can a prayer be counted which has lost its spirit and essence, and only its form and outward appearance remain?

They said: And if the servant deliberately abandons one of its obligatory elements, his abandoning it invalidates it. At best, it is like a part of its parts, comparable to the loss of a limb of the slave being freed in an expiation (kaffarah). So how much more so when it has lost its spirit, its essence and its purpose? It becomes like a dead slave: if a slave with a severed hand is not counted when one frees him as a drawing near to Allah the Exalted in an obligatory expiation, how then can a dead slave be counted?

Some of the early scholars (salaf) said: Prayer is like a slave-girl presented to a king. What then is thought of the one who presents to him a paralysed slave-girl, or a blind one, or one with a severed hand and foot, or a sick one, or an ugly one, or a hideous one, until he presents to him a dead slave-girl without spirit? How, then, of the prayer which the servant presents and by which he draws near to his Lord, the Exalted? Allah is good and accepts only what is good, and a prayer without spirit is not among good deeds, just as the freeing of a slave without spirit is not among good manumissions.

They said: Leaving the heart idle from the worship of presence and humility is leaving the king of the limbs idle from his worship and removing him from it. What then avails the obedience and worship of the subjects when their king has been dismissed and made idle?

They said: The limbs follow the heart; they are made sound by its soundness and corrupted by its corruption. If it is not standing in its worship, then the limbs are even less entitled to have their worship counted. And if its worship is corrupted by heedlessness and whisperings, how can the worship of its subjects, its soldiers and its supplies from it, and by whose command they act and by whom they are directed, be valid?

They said: In al-Tirmidhi and others, it is related as a marfu' hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah does not answer the supplication of a heedless heart." This is either specific to the supplication of worship, or general to it and to the supplication of request, or specific to the supplication of request, which is the more remote. It is an indication that He does not accept the supplication of worship, which is specifically His right, from a heedless heart.

They said: Because the worship of one whose heedlessness and forgetfulness predominate is generally not accompanied by sincerity (ikhlas), for sincerity is intending the worshipped alone with the worship. The heedless has no intention, so he has no worship.

They said: Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿So woe to those who pray, who are heedless of their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'un: 4]. Heedlessness of it is not abandoning it, otherwise they would not be described as praying. It is rather heedlessness of its obligatory elements, either of the time, as Ibn Mas'ud and others said, or of presence and humility. The correct view is that it encompasses both kinds, for He, glorified is He, affirmed for them a prayer and described them as heedless of it. So it is heedlessness of its obligatory time, or of its obligatory sincerity and presence. For this reason He described them as showing off, and if the heedlessness were heedlessness of abandonment there would be no showing off.

They said: Even if we suppose that it is heedlessness of an obligatory element only, it is an alert to the threat of woe for heedlessness of sincerity and presence, by way of a fortiori argument, for several reasons:

The first: the time obligation drops in a state of excuse and is replaced by its substitute, whereas sincerity and presence never drop in any state and have no substitute.

The second: the obligation of the time drops to complete the benefit of presence, so combining two prayers is permitted for an occupation that prevents performing one of them in its time without heart or presence, such as the traveller, the sick, and one with a burden that requires combining, as Ahmad and others explicitly stated.

In sum: the benefit of sincerity and presence, and the gathering of the heart upon Allah in prayer, is weightier in the view of the Lawgiver than the benefit of all its other obligations. How then could it be supposed that He would invalidate it by abandoning one takbir, or one standing-upright in a pillar, or the omission of a letter or a shaddah in the Qur'an, or the omission of one tasbih, or of "Allah hears the one who praises Him," or of "Our Lord, and to You be praise," or of the mention of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with blessings upon him; and then validate it despite the loss of its essence, its supreme purpose, its spirit and its secret?

This is what this group argued, and these arguments, as you see, are strong and evident.

The proponents of the other view said: It is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) in the Sahih that he said: "When the muezzin calls the adhan, Satan turns his back and has a fart, so that he does not hear the adhan. When the adhan is finished, he returns. When the iqamah is called, he turns his back again. When the iqamah is finished, he returns, until he whispers between a man and himself, reminding him of what he did not remember, and saying: Remember such-and-such, remember such-and-such, of what he did not used to recall, until a man does not know how many (rak'ahs) he has prayed. When one of you experiences that, let him prostrate twice while sitting."

They said: The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded, in this prayer in which Satan had distracted him so that he did not know how much he had prayed, that he perform the two prostrations of forgetfulness, and he did not command him to repeat it. Had it been invalid as you claim, he would have commanded him to repeat it.

They said: This is the secret of the two prostrations of forgetfulness: to humiliate Satan for his whispering to the servant and for his coming between him and presence in prayer. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) called them "al-murghimatan" (the two that humiliate the enemy), and he commanded whoever forgot to perform them, and he did not distinguish in the forgetfulness which caused the obligation of prostration between the little and the much, or the dominant and the subdued, and he said: "For every forgetfulness there are two prostrations," and he did not exempt from that the dominant forgetfulness, even though it is the dominant one.

They said: Also, the laws of Islam are based on outward actions, whereas the inner realities of faith are subject to the laws of reward and punishment. So Allah has two rulings: a ruling in this world based on outward laws and the actions of the limbs, and a ruling in the Hereafter based on outward and inward matters. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) would accept the outward profession of the hypocrites and leave their secrets to Allah, so they married and inherited and were inherited from, and their prayers were counted in the rulings of this world, so their ruling was not the ruling of one who abandons prayer, since they had brought its outward form. The rulings of reward and punishment are not for mankind but for Allah, and Allah will take charge of them in the Hereafter.

Yes, the purpose of this prayer, the reward of Allah, whether immediate or deferred, is not attained, for prayer has an additional immediate reward in the heart: the strength of faith, its illumination, its opening and expansion, the sweetness of worship, joy, gladness, and the delight that comes to one whose concern and heart are gathered upon Allah and whose heart is present before Him, just as one who is brought near by a sultan and singled out for his intimate conversation and attention experiences. Allah is higher and more exalted.

Likewise, what he attains of the high ranks in the Hereafter and companionship with those brought near.

All of this is lost with the loss of presence and humility. Two men may stand in the same row, yet the distance between their two prayers is like that between heaven and earth. Our discussion is not about all of this.

If you mean that repetition is obligatory so that these fruits and benefits may be attained, then that is up to him: if he wishes to attain them, and if he wishes to forfeit them for himself. But if you mean by its obligation that we compel him to it and punish him for abandoning it, and apply to him the rulings of one who abandons prayer, then no.

This second view is the stronger of the two opinions, and Allah knows best.

(Faidah)

The financial rights owed to Allah Most High are of four categories:

The first: rights of property, such as zakat. This is established as a debt upon the person once he is able to pay it. If he becomes unable to pay it after that, it is not waived; but if he is unable at the time it becomes obligatory, it is not established as a debt upon him. Zakat al-fitr is attached to this category.

The second category: what becomes obligatory because of an expiation (kaffarah), such as the expiation for oaths, for zihar, for intercourse during Ramadan, and the expiation for killing. If he is unable to fulfil it at the time its causes arise, there are two well-known opinions in the school of al-Shafi'i and Ahmad: whether it remains as a debt upon him until he is able (al-maysarah), or whether it is waived.

The third category: what carries the meaning of compensation for destroyed property, such as the penalty (jaza') for hunting game, and attached to it is the ransom (fidyah) for shaving, perfume, and clothing while in ihram. If he is unable to pay it at the time it becomes obligatory, it is established as a debt upon him, giving precedence to the meaning of indemnity and compensation for what has been destroyed. This is clear in the case of game.

As for perfume and its like, the matter is not the same, because it is a matter of comfort, not destruction. Hair and nails are not destroyed by removal, and the ransom for removing them was not made obligatory in exchange for destruction; for if it were obligatory because it is destruction, it would be restricted by value, and they have no value. Rather, it belongs purely to the category of comfort, like covering the head and wearing clothing, so where is the destruction here?

On this basis, the preponderant of the opinions is that the fidyah is not obligatory in cases of forgetfulness and ignorance.

The fourth category: the sacrifice of nusuk (hady) such as that of tamattu' and qiran. If he is unable to offer it, its substitute becomes obligatory, which is fasting. If he is unable to fast as well, one of them remains as a debt upon him: whenever he is able to fulfil it, it becomes binding upon him. Whether the consideration is the state at the time of obligation or the most severe of states is a matter of disagreement.

As for the rights of human beings, they are not waived by inability to fulfil them. But if his inability is due to negligence on his part in discharging them, then in the Hereafter they will be taken from him and given to their owners from his good deeds. If his inability is not due to negligence, such as one whose property was burned or drowned, or where the destruction was by mistake while he is unable to compensate for it, then whether his obligation remains as a debt upon him and their owners take from his good deeds is open to consideration. I have not found a satisfactory statement from the scholars on this matter. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 23, verse 5–7:

He (glorified is He) made the success of the servant contingent upon guarding his private parts from [unlawful use], so there is no path to success without it. He said: ﴿Successful indeed are the believers, who are humble in their prayer, who turn away from ill speech, who are active in giving zakat, who guard their private parts, except from their wives or those their right hands possess, for then they are not blameworthy. But whoever seeks beyond that, it is they who are the transgressors.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1–7] up to His saying.

This contains three matters: that whoever does not guard his private parts is not among the successful, that he is among the blameworthy, and that he is among the transgressors. Thus he loses success, deserves the name of aggression, and falls into blame. The suffering of the pain of desire and its struggle is easier than some of that.

[Section: The wisdom in permitting the master to enjoy his female slave but not permitting the slave to enjoy his mistress]

As for his statement: "He permitted the man to enjoy his female slave by right of ownership, by intercourse and otherwise, and did not permit the woman to enjoy her slave, neither by intercourse nor otherwise," this too is part of the perfection and wisdom of this Law. The master dominates his slave, rules over him, and owns him, and the husband dominates his wife and rules over her, while she is under his authority and rule, like a captive. For this reason He prohibited the slave from marrying his mistress, because of the incompatibility between his being her slave and her husband, and between her being his mistress and the one he has intercourse with.
