What remains is to ask: the hadith of Hudhayfah indicates that the beginning of the formation is after the first forty, while the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud indicates that it is after the third forty. How can they be reconciled?

It is said: as for the hadith of Hudhayfah, it is explicit that this takes place after the forty. As for the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, it contains no reference to the time of shaping and formation; it only explains the stages of the drop and its transformations after every forty, and that after the third forty the spirit is breathed into it. The hadith of Hudhayfah does not address this, but it is specific to the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud. So the two hadiths share the occurrence of a matter after the first forty. The hadith of Hudhayfah is specific in that the beginning of its shaping and creation is after the first forty, and the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud is specific in that the breathing of the spirit into it is after the third forty. The two hadiths share the angel's seeking permission from his Lord, Glorified is He, to determine the state of the child during that period. Thus the words of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) agree, and some of them confirm others.

The hadith of Ibn Mas'ud contains two matters: the matter of the drop and its transformations, and the matter of the angel's writing what Allah decrees concerning it. The Prophet (ﷺ) informed of both matters in the hadith. Imam Ahmad said: "Hushaym related to us: Ali ibn Zayd informed us: I heard Abu Utbah ibn Abdullah narrate: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

'Indeed the drop remains in the womb for forty days in its condition, not changing. When forty have passed for it, it becomes a clot, then a lump of flesh in the same manner, then bones in the same manner. When He wills to fashion its creation, Allah sends to it the angel, who says, the angel charged with it: O Lord, male or female? Wretched or blessed? Short or tall? Deficient or complete? Its sustenance and its term? Healthy or sick? He says: and he writes all of that.'"

This hadith contains the cure, and what occurs after the third forty is the fashioning of the creation at the time of the breathing of the spirit into it.

There is no doubt that at the breathing of the spirit into it and its attachment to it, there occurs in its creation matters additional to the formation that was after the first forty. The first was the beginning of the formation, and this is its perfecting and the completion of what was decreed for it, just as Allah, Glorified is He, created the earth before the heaven, then created the heaven, then after that arranged the earth, spread it out and completed its creation. That is His action in the dwelling-place, and this is His action in the one who dwells in it. Moreover, the formation and shaping arise in the drop after the forty gradually, bit by bit, as plants grow. This is observed in animals and plants, as when you consider the state of the chick in the egg. The confusion arises only from failing to understand the words of Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ). The confusion is in our understanding, not in the explanation of the infallible one.

And Allah is the One whose help is sought. This has sufficed you, praise be to Allah, from the labored efforts of the commentators, so ponder it, weigh it against this combined view, and with Allah is success.

(Section)

Hippocrates said in his book *al-Ghidha* (On Nutrition): The shaping of the fetus occurs in thirty-five days, its first movement in seventy days, and its completion in one hundred and ten days. Other fetuses are shaped in fifty days, and they move with the first movement at one hundred days, and they complete at three hundred. Other fetuses are shaped in forty days, they move at eighty days, and they are born at two hundred and forty days. Other fetuses are shaped in forty-five days, they move at ninety days, and they are born at two hundred and seventy days. He said: As for birth, it occurs in the seventh, eighth, ninth and tenth months.

I say: Movement is of two kinds. One is natural, involuntary movement, and this occurs before the attachment of the spirit to it. As for voluntary movement, it does not occur except after the breathing of the spirit. For this reason Hippocrates distinguished between the first and the second movement.

I say: What the true revelation has indicated about the Creator of mankind is that creation passes through a new stage every forty days. It is first a drop for forty days, then a clot for the same, then a lump for the same, then the spirit is breathed into it after one hundred and twenty days.

This is as though you were witnessing it directly. Whatever contradicts it has no direct observation behind it. The most that he has is a flawed analogy and an anatomical examination that does not encompass knowledge of the origin of what he observed, or the imitation of a single non-infallible person. Everything that came from him was followed by others who accepted it. The one who believes in it thinks it is a matter agreed upon among the naturalists, while its root is one error, which the first man made and then others imitated after him. Those people did not witness what they reported about it.

The most they have is that they dissected pregnant women, living and dead, and found the fetus in the womb in the form they described. But they have no knowledge of what lies beyond that, such as the beginning of pregnancy and the changes in the state of the drop. Suppose their imitator were to press the point:

We may assume that they observed a virgin from the time she was penetrated, then counted her days until she reached what they mentioned, then dissected her and found the matter in the form they described. This is the utmost lie and slander, for those people did not claim this, and how could they claim it when they report that after so many days the state of the pregnancy will become such and such? What they have is universals and analogies: it should be such and such, and the natural order requires such and such.

Many of them derive it from the movements of the moon, its waxing and waning, and from the movements of the sun, and from the trine, the quadrature, the sextile and the opposition. Others among them refuted them and nullified this against them in many respects. Some referred it to what is more proper, more suitable and more fitting. Others referred it to the days of the seas and the change of their nature. Some of these refuted others and nullified their statements with what we have omitted for fear of prolixity.

The soundest of what they have is dissection and complete induction, which admit no exception. We do not deny that, but there is nothing in it that contradicts revelation concerning the differences among fetuses at all. Among the things that show that these people did not report this from direct observation is their saying that the fetus born in the seventh month becomes a *daydiyyan* (the stage of the seminal drop) in nine days, then *damawiyyan* (the stage of blood) in eight other days, then *lahmiyyan* (the stage of flesh) in nine other days, and receives the form in twelve other days. When these days are added together they make thirty-five days, so they made it a lump of flesh within the first forty.

This is clearly and certainly a lie. The fetus becomes flesh only after the eightieth day. Such a matter cannot be known except by revelation or direct observation, and both are absent from them. What they have is an analogy by which they inferred the states of fetuses from the months of their birth. They then judged that every fetus born in a month of the birth months should be a *daydiyyan*, that is, a drop of such and such a number of days, a *damawiyyan*, that is, a clot of such and such a number of days, and a *lahmiyyan*, that is, a lump of such and such a number of days. Then they halved that number and made it the time of the fetus's movement.

They lied about the All-Knowing Creator in His creation, as they lied about Him in His attributes and names. Those people had no share of the knowledge that the messengers brought. Rather, they were, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So when their messengers came to them with clear proofs, they rejoiced in what knowledge they had﴾. What does the one who rejects and turns away from what the messengers brought attain? The most he attains is knowledge of natural matters, in which there is truth and falsehood, and mathematical matters that involve much labor and little benefit, and astronomical matters whose falsehood is many times their truth. How far is the knowledge received from the descending revelation from the opinion derived from a fleeting view? How far is the knowledge taken from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), from Jibril, from Allah the Mighty and Majestic, from the opinion taken from the view of a man whose heart has not been illumined by the light of revelation for a moment of an eye? He has only his intuition and his guessing. The attachment of what all rational people perceive by their intellects to what the messengers brought is like the relation of a weak lamp to the light of the sun.

You will not find, even if you lived the lifespan of Noah, a single question on which all rational people agree against what the messengers brought in any matter whatsoever. The prophets did not bring anything that contradicts clear reason at all. Rather, they brought what reason cannot perceive. What the messengers brought, alongside reason, falls into three categories with no fourth: a category which reason and natural disposition attest to; a category which reason attests to in general but does not guide to its details; and a category for which reason has no capacity to perceive. As for the fourth category, that which clear reason deems impossible and attests to its falsehood, the messengers are free of it. Yet many ignorant people who claim knowledge and insight think that some of what the messengers brought belongs to this category. This is either because of their ignorance of what the messengers brought, or their ignorance of the judgment of reason, or both.

(Section)

On the states of the fetus after its movement and its transformation at the completion of half a year. At this time it happens to the fetus that its membrane and the veils around it are torn, and that it moves from its place toward the mouth of the womb. If the fetus is strong and its membranes and its umbilical cord are weaker, the birth is complete. If the fetus is weak while its membranes and umbilical cord are stronger, then either they are torn in part and it is not born, so it remains sick for forty days until the end of the eighth month completes...

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 23, verse 12–16 (part 3 of 3):

If the child is born during these forty days, it dies, and neither its upbringing nor its survival is possible. If its membranes are torn completely, so that it cannot be saved from this, and it is not born, it dies; and if it does not miscarry, the pregnant woman is killed. If its membranes are torn in a way that can be remedied, it remains and does not die, and it stays in its place toward which it moved and turned, at the mouth of the womb. Illness afflicts them during these forty days if they are not born after they have moved, because they turn over from the place in which they grew and their positions change, and the navel is dislodged by its movement. Also, their mothers may fall ill at that time because of the stretching of the membranes and the dislodging of the navel that is connected to the womb in them. Also, when the fetus's bond is loosened, it becomes heavy upon its mother.

(Section)

When the fetus has been formed and the Creator, the Fashioner, has shaped it, it is created with its head upward and its legs downward. When God permits its emergence, it turns over and its head comes to be downward, so its head precedes the rest of its body. This is agreed upon by physicians and anatomists, and this is part of the perfection of divine care for the fetus and its mother, because when its head comes out first, the emergence of the rest of its body is easier, without any part of them needing to bend. For if the fetus's legs came out first, it could not be assured that it would become caught in the womb at its hands; and if one of its legs came out, it could not be assured that it would become hooked and caught in the womb as it develops. If both hands came out, it could not be assured that it would become caught at its head, either because it twists backward, or because the navel twists around its neck or shoulder, since when the fetus descends and reaches a place where the navel is stretched, it twists there around its neck and shoulder. Thus, from that, one of two things results: either the navel pulls at it, so the mother suffers extreme pain, and then the fetus either dies or its emergence is difficult, and it comes out sick and swollen. So the wisdom of the Most Wise of judges required that it turn over in the belly, so that its head comes out first and the rest of the body follows the head.

(Section)

Concerning the reason why a child born at eight months does not survive, while one born at seven, nine, or ten months does survive.

When the fetus completes seven months, it develops a strong movement, which it makes naturally for turning and emerging. If the fetus is strong among those children who have by nature great strength in their constitution and make-up, so that by its movement it is able to tear the membranes surrounding it that are connected to the womb, until it passes through and emerges from them, it comes out in the seventh month strong, healthy and sound, the movement not having harmed it and the turning not having made it ill. But if it is too weak for that, then either it perishes because of the harm and pain it suffers from the movement of turning, and comes out dead, or it remains in the belly and becomes ill, and remains in its illness for about forty days until it recovers, revives and grows strong. When it is born within the eighth month, it is born while still ill, not having been freed from its pain, so it perishes and does not survive and is not raised. But if it remains in the womb until it passes these forty days into the ninth month, and grows strong, revives, and its time of illness is far behind it, it is likely to survive; and those most deserving of survival are those who remained longest in the womb after the turning, namely those born in the tenth month. As for those born between the tenth and ninth months, their condition in this respect is according to nearness and distance.

Another scholar said: the reason that a child born at eight months cannot survive is that two kinds of harm follow upon it: one is its turning in the seventh month within the womb for birth, and the second is the change of condition between its place in the womb and its place in the air. Although this change may happen to all fetuses, the child born at seven months escapes from the womb before the harm within it reaches him, following the turning and the illnesses that occur inside the womb. The child born at seven months and at ten months remains in the womb until it recovers and is saved from those illnesses, so the two harms do not follow upon it together. The child born at eight months has the two harms following upon it together, and therefore it cannot survive, since all fetuses in the eighth month are afflicted with illness.

What indicates this is that you find all pregnant women in the eighth month in a worse condition and heavier than in the months before this month and after it, and the conditions of mothers are connected to the conditions of the fetuses.

(Section)

The crying of a child at the hour of its birth indicates its health, strength and vigor. When the child places its hand, thumb or finger on a limb of its body, this is a sign of pain in that limb. Every animal by nature indicates what pains it in its body, either with its paw, its mouth, its head or its tail. So when the child lacks speech, it points with its finger or hand to the place of its pain, like a dumb animal.

(Section)

Concerning how children, while in the womb, are stronger than they are after their birth, more patient and more able to bear what befalls them. Likewise, the care for them after their birth is more emphatic and the caution for them is greater. For the branches of a tree and its boughs, as long as they are adhering to the tree and connected to it, are hardly shaken or uprooted by violent winds; but when they are separated from it and planted in other places, they are struck by calamity and reached by the slightest wind that blows, until it uproots them. Likewise, the fetus, as long as it is in the womb, grows strong and patient against what befalls it and what it suffers from poor management and harm, more than it can bear even the slightest of these after its birth and separation from the womb. Likewise, the fruit on the tree is stronger and more firm than after it is cut from it.

Since separation from everything customary and familiar, by moving away from it, is very difficult for the one who undertakes it, especially when the move is all at once, the fetus, upon separation from the womb, moves at once from what it has become accustomed to and familiar with in all its conditions, and the severity of this move upon it is greater than the severity of a move by gradual stages.

For this reason Hippocrates said: "It may be known with the least effort and ease that bad regimen of food and drink, if it continues in one unchanging manner, resembling itself always, is more reliable, safer and further from danger in seeking health for bodies than if a man changes his regimen all at once to a better food." The fetus moves from what it has become accustomed to in its nourishment, breathing, entrances and what surrounds it, in a single instant.

This is the first hardship it meets in the world, after which hardships gather around it until the last of them is the supreme hardship beyond which there is no hardship, or the supreme ease beyond which there is no weariness. For this reason it does not cry at the arrival of this hardship upon it, along with what it meets of the Satan's prodding and his jab in its side.

(Section)

The fetus in the womb was nourished by what suited it, and by nature it drew from its mother's blood the amount suited to it. After its emergence it likewise draws from milk what suits it, but it draws by its appetite and will, so it exceeds the amount it needs, while the milk may be bad and diseased just as it may be sound. Likewise it suffers vomiting and nausea, and it draws in the humors of its body, and it is afflicted with pains, aches and calamities that did not befall it in the belly. In the belly it had membranes and veils that prevented harm from reaching it; but when it was born, it was provided with other membranes and veils to which it was not accustomed or habituated, and it is sometimes exposed to heat, cold and wind. It draws from its navel, which is the most delicate, most temperate and healthiest thing, the very thing that keeps the mother's heart and pulsing veins sound. So it resembles one who enters a bath and draws in the delicate, temperate air, and then comes out of it all at once, naked, into the harsh and harmful wind.

In sum, it has moved away from what it was used to and accustomed to, all at once, to something more severe and difficult for it. This is part of the perfect wisdom of the All-Creating, the All-Knowing, to train His servant to leave his habits and familiar things for what is better, more beneficial and more suitable for him. God, exalted is He, pointed to this in His saying: ﴿You shall surely ride from stage to stage﴾ [al-Inshiqaq 84:19], meaning state after state. Its first stages are that it is a drop of semen, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then a fetus, then a newborn, then a suckling, then weaned, then healthy or sick, rich or poor, safe or afflicted, through all the various conditions of man upon him, until he dies, then is resurrected, then is made to stand before God, Exalted, then he goes to Paradise or to the Fire. So the meaning is: you shall ride from state to state, from station to station, and from matter to matter.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Zayd said: "You shall surely be in the Hereafter after the first life, and you shall surely become rich after poverty and poor after wealth."

'Ata' said: "Hardship after hardship." And "tabaq" and "tabaqah" mean the state. For this reason it is said: "So-and-so was in various tabaqat," i.e., various states.

'Amr ibn al-'As said: "I was in three tabaqat," meaning three states.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: "The tabaq is the state, in its variations."

We have mentioned some of the stages of the fetus in the belly from the time it was a drop until the time of its birth. Now we mention its stages after its birth until their end, so we say:

The fetus in the womb is like the fruit on the tree in its strong connection to its place. When it reaches its completion, nothing remains but its separation, because of its weight and maturity, and the severing of the veins that hold it. Likewise, the fetus: those membranes are torn away, and the veins that hold it between the placenta and the womb are severed, and those slippery fluids become the means of easing its exit through their slipperiness; its weight and the tearing of the veins aid its emergence. The womb opens very widely, and some great joints must separate, then they rejoin in the quickest time. Skilled physicians and anatomists have acknowledged this, and they said that this is not accomplished except by divine care and a design that defeats the minds of people in grasping how it is done: ﴿So blessed is God, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:14].

When the fetus is separated, it cries at the moment of its separation, for a natural reason, which is its parting from what it was familiar with and its place in which it was, and for an external cause, which is the Satan's jab in its side. When it is separated and its separation is complete, it stretches its hand to its mouth. When forty days have passed for it, you find it having another matter similar to what was renewed for it while in the womb, and it laughs at forty days, and that is the first time it perceives itself. When it has two months, it sees dreams. Then discernment and intellect develop with it gradually, little by little, until the age of discernment. There is no fixed age for this; among people there is one who discerns at five, as Mahmud ibn al-Rabi' said: "I remember from the Prophet ﷺ a mouthful he spat into my face from a bucket in their well, and I was the son of five years."

For this reason the age of five has been set as the limit of the child's keen hearing.

Some discern at less than that, and remember things that happened to them while under five years old.

It has been mentioned of Iyas ibn Mu'awiya that he said: "Remember the day my mother bore me, for I came out from darkness into light, then I went into darkness again." His mother was asked about that, and she said: "He spoke truly. When he was separated from me, I did not have anything to make him familiar with it, so I placed a bowl over him."

This is among the most wondrous and rare of things. When he reaches seven years, he enters the age of discernment and is commanded to pray,

as in the Musnad and the Sunan, from the hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said:

"Command your children to pray at seven years old, and strike them for it at ten years old, and separate them in their beds."

(Section)

Every pleasure that is followed by pain, or that prevents a greater pleasure, is not truly a pleasure, even if the soul is deceived into enjoying it. What pleasure is there for one who eats delicious poisoned food that will soon cut through his intestines? These are the pleasures of the disbelievers and the corrupt, in their exaltation on earth, their corruption, and their rejoicing in it without right, and their exultation.

Such is the pleasure of the eye. They took, besides Allah, protectors whom they love as they love Allah, and they gained affection among themselves in the life of this world. Then that pleasure turned into the greatest and most bitter pain.

Among this is the pleasure of corrupt beliefs and rejoicing in them, and the pleasure of the dominance of the oppressive, the unjust, the aggressors, adulterers, thieves, and drinkers of intoxicants. Allah, glorified and exalted, has informed us that He did not enable them to do this out of good that He intends for them; rather it is a gradual lure by which He will bring upon them the greatest pain. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Do they reckon that what We extend to them of wealth and children is a hastening of good for them? Nay, they do not perceive.﴾

And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So let not their wealth nor their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them thereby in the life of this world, and that their souls depart while they are disbelievers.﴾

As for the pleasure that does not bring pain in the abode of permanence and does not lead to a pleasure there, it is a vain pleasure, having neither benefit nor harm, its duration is brief, and the soul has no real enjoyment of it. It will inevitably distract from what is better and more beneficial than it in this world and the next, even if it does not distract from the essential pleasure in the Hereafter. This is the category that the Prophet ﷺ meant by his saying: "Every diversion with which a man amuses himself is vain, except his shooting with his bow, his training of his horse, and his playing with his wife, for these are from the truth."

Related by Muslim.

Therefore, playing the tambourine at a wedding is permissible, for it assists in marriage, just as the pleasure of archery and training horses assists in jihad. Both are beloved to Allah, and whatever aids the attainment of what is beloved to Him is from the truth. For this reason, a man's playing with his wife is counted as from the truth, since it aids her in the purposes of marriage, which Allah, glorified and exalted, loves. Whatever does not aid what the Lord, exalted is He, loves is vain and of no benefit. However, if it contains no overriding harm, it is not forbidden nor prohibited. But if it diverts from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer, it becomes disliked, hateful to the Lord, abhorrent in His sight, either by its very nature or by excess in it. Every pleasure that diverts from the desired pleasure is a burden upon its owner, for if he, while engaged in it, were occupied with what benefits him and brings the desired lasting pleasure, it would be better and more beneficial for him. Since weak souls, such as those of women and children, do not submit to the causes of the greatest pleasure unless they are given some of the pleasure of amusement and play, such that if they were weaned from it entirely they would seek what is worse for them, they are granted a dispensation in this matter that is not granted to others.

This is like when Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, entered upon the Prophet ﷺ while there were slave girls beside him beating the tambourine. He silenced them upon his entry and said: "This is a man who does not love falsehood."

He informed that this is vain, yet he did not forbid them from it, due to the overriding benefit that accrues to them from it, and they forgo through it a greater harm than its harm.

Also, the distress they would suffer from abandoning it would be a greater harm than the harm of it, so permitting them to do it is out of mercy, compassion, and kindness, just as the Prophet ﷺ permitted Abu Umayr to play with the sparrow in his presence, permitted the two girls to sing in his presence, permitted Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, to look at the Abyssinians playing in the mosque, permitted that woman to strike the tambourine over his head, and similar cases.

How far is this from the practice of those shaykhs referred to, who took this as their religion and path, the Sufi masters followed, while expanding it to the utmost extent, in what there is no doubt about its prohibition.

A parallel to this is the Prophet's ﷺ giving to those whose hearts are to be reconciled (al-mu'allafa qulubuhum) from the zakat and the spoils, due to the weakness of their hearts compared to the hearts of the firmly rooted in faith among his companions. For this reason he gave to these and withheld from those, and he said: "I entrust them to what Allah has placed in their hearts of contentment and goodness."

A parallel to this is his ﷺ jesting with those who joked with him among the Bedouins, the children, and the women, to delight their hearts, win their faith, and cheer them.

In the mursal narrations of al-Sha'bi, the Prophet ﷺ passed by people playing the daraklah, and said: "Take it easy, O sons of Arfada, so that the Jews and Christians may know that there is latitude in our religion." Abu Ubayd related it, and said that the daraklah is a game of the non-Arabs (ajam). The Prophet ﷺ thus gives souls wealth and benefits by which he reconciles them to the truth that he was commanded to convey, and what is given is something the recipient takes pleasure in and loves, because that is a means to something else. He does not do this with those who do not need it, such as the Muhajirun and the Ansar; rather he gives them other kinds of kindness and benefits in their religion and their worldly affairs. Since Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, was one who did not love this falsehood nor to hear it, and did not need to be reconciled by what others were reconciled by, and was not commanded with what the Prophet ﷺ was commanded regarding reconciling people to belief in him and obedience to him by every means, his aversion to it was a perfection in relation to him, while the Prophet's ﷺ state was more perfect.

Also, the distress they would suffer from abandoning it would be a greater harm than the harm of it, so permitting them to do it is out of mercy, compassion, and kindness, just as the Prophet ﷺ permitted Abu Umayr to play with the sparrow in his presence, permitted the two girls to sing in his presence, permitted Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, to look at the Abyssinians playing in the mosque, permitted that woman to strike the tambourine over his head, and similar cases.

How far is this from the practice of those shaykhs referred to, who took this as their religion and path, the Sufi masters followed, while expanding it to the utmost extent, in what there is no doubt about its prohibition.

A parallel to this is the Prophet's ﷺ giving to those whose hearts are to be reconciled (al-mu'allafa qulubuhum) from the zakat and the spoils, due to the weakness of their hearts compared to the hearts of the firmly rooted in faith among his companions. For this reason he gave to these and withheld from those, and he said: "I entrust them to what Allah has placed in their hearts of contentment and goodness."

A parallel to this is his ﷺ jesting with those who joked with him among the Bedouins, the children, and the women, to delight their hearts, win their faith, and cheer them.

In the mursal narrations of al-Sha'bi, the Prophet ﷺ passed by people playing the daraklah, and said: "Take it easy, O sons of Arfada, so that the Jews and Christians may know that there is latitude in our religion." Abu Ubayd related it, and said that the daraklah is a game of the non-Arabs (ajam). The Prophet ﷺ thus gives souls wealth and benefits by which he reconciles them to the truth that he was commanded to convey, and what is given is something the recipient takes pleasure in and loves, because that is a means to something else. He does not do this with those who do not need it, such as the Muhajirun and the Ansar; rather he gives them other kinds of kindness and benefits in their religion and their worldly affairs. Since Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, was one who did not love this falsehood nor to hear it, and did not need to be reconciled by what others were reconciled by, and was not commanded with what the Prophet ﷺ was commanded regarding reconciling people to belief in him and obedience to him by every means, his aversion to it was a perfection in relation to him, while the Prophet's ﷺ state was more perfect.

[Section: Fear Produces Scrupulousness]

Fear produces *wara'* (scrupulousness, avoiding the doubtful), seeking help (from Allah), and shortening of hope. The strength of faith in the meeting (with Allah) produces *zuhd* (asceticism, renunciation of the world). Knowledge produces love, fear, and hope. Contentment produces satisfaction. Remembrance produces the life of the heart.

Repentance also produces love, and continual remembrance produces it. Satisfaction produces gratitude. Resolve and patience produce all states and stations (*maqamat*).

Sincerity (*ikhlas*) and truthfulness (*sidq*) each produce and require the other.

Knowledge produces good character. Reflection produces resolve.

The first: that you move your heart from the homeland of this world and settle it in the homeland of the Hereafter. Allah has a guardian and protector over it who watches over those who travel it, shields them, and repels harm from them. None knows the value of this path except one who knows the ways of people, their dangers, their calamities, and their highwaymen. And Allah is the One sought for help.

[Section: The Second Degree of the Degrees of Sincerity: Shame at One's Deeds Together with Exerting One's Utmost Effort]

The author of *al-Manazil* (Abu Isma'il al-Ansari) said:

"The second degree: shame at one's deeds, together with exerting one's utmost effort, preserving one's striving by shielding oneself from witnessing (one's own action), and seeing the deed in the light of success from the source of generosity."

These are three matters: his "shame" at his deed, which is the intensity of his modesty before Allah, since he does not see that deed as worthy of Him, despite having exerted his effort in it. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful that they will return to their Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 60].

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is the man who fasts, prays, and gives charity, and fears that it will not be accepted from him."

Some of them said: "I pray two rak'ahs, and then I stand after them like a thief or an adulterer whom people see, out of modesty before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic."

So the believer combines good works with fear and with a poor opinion of himself. The deceived person has a good opinion of himself while he is in fact doing evil.

The second: preserving one's effort by shielding oneself from witnessing, meaning that he works with the utmost of his capacity to correct the deed, while guarding against witnessing it as coming from himself or by himself.

The third: that you shelter yourself in the light of success, with which Allah illuminates the insight of the servant. So in the light of that illumination you see that your deed comes from the source of His generosity, not by you, nor from you.

This degree thus contains five things: a deed, striving in it, shame, modesty before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, guarding oneself from witnessing it as coming from oneself, and seeing it as coming from the source of Allah's generosity, glorified is He, and from Him.

[Section: The Second Degree of the Degrees of Character: Improving Your Character Toward the Truth]

He said: "The second degree: improving your character toward the Truth. Its improvement from your side is that you know that everything that comes from you calls for an excuse, that everything that comes from the Truth calls for gratitude, and that you do not see any escape from fulfilling this."

This degree is built on two principles.

The first: that you know you are deficient, and whatever comes from a deficient being is deficient. So it necessarily requires him to apologize for it. The servant must seek to excuse himself before his Lord for everything he does, good or bad. As for the bad, it is obvious. As for the good, he apologizes for its shortcomings, and does not see it as worthy of his Lord.

So he, despite his good deeds, is apologetic about his good deeds. For this reason Allah praised His friends for their fear of Him despite their good deeds, saying: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 60]. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is the man who fasts and gives charity, and fears that it will not be accepted from him." So when he fears, he is more deserving of apologizing.

What moves him to this apology are two matters:

The first: witnessing his negligence and shortcoming.

The second: the sincerity of his love.

For the sincere lover draws near to his beloved with the utmost of his ability. He apologizes to Him and is shy before Him, that he might confront Him with what He has confronted him with. He sees that His rank is above him and more majestic than him. This is observed in love among created beings.

The second principle: magnifying everything that comes from Him, glorified is He, to you, and acknowledging that it calls for your gratitude, and that you are incapable of thanking Him. This is only made clear in true love, for the lover considers much of what he receives from his beloved.

If He mentions something to him and gives it to him, his joy at being mentioned by Him and at being deemed worthy of His gift is greater to him than his joy at the gift itself. Indeed, his joy at being mentioned by his beloved overshadows his joy at the gift. The lover is pleased by his beloved's mention of him even if he receives it with something displeasing.

As the poet said:

*If it grieves me that you have struck me with a harm,*
*it has delighted me that I came to your mind.*

How much more so when the beloved bestows upon him a joy, however small. He sees it only as great and momentous. How then is this with the Lord, exalted is He, who never brings anything except good, and for whom the opposite is impossible? Just as the opposite of His perfection is impossible for Him.

The one who knows Allah best, the Prophet (ﷺ), has made this clear in his saying: "And evil is not attributed to You."

That is, it is not to be ascribed to You, nor attributed to You, nor issuing from You. For His Names are all beautiful, His Attributes are all perfection, and His actions are all grace and justice, wisdom and mercy, and benefit. In what way, then, could evil be ascribed to Him, glorified and exalted is He? Everything that comes from Him is due praise and thanks from Him, and in it is His blessing and bounty.

His saying: "and that you do not see any escape from fulfilling this" means: your treatment of the Truth, glorified is He, according to the requirement of apologizing for everything from yourself, and thanking Him for everything from Him, is a covenant with Allah, the Exalted, binding upon you forever. You do not see any escape from fulfilling it.

This is not a passing matter or a state that changes. Rather, it is a binding covenant upon you to fulfill until the Day of Resurrection.

[Section: Hope and Wishful Thinking]

It is fitting that whoever hopes for something, his hope entails three matters:

The first: love of what he hopes for.

The second: fear of losing it.

The third: striving to attain it to the extent of his ability.

As for a hope that is not accompanied by any of these, it is among wishful thinking (*amani*). Hope is one thing, and wishful thinking is another. Every one who hopes is also fearful, and the traveler on the road, when he fears, hastens his journey for fear of missing (his destination).

In the Jami' of at-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever fears sets out at night, and whoever sets out at night reaches the destination. Indeed, the commodity of Allah is precious. Indeed, the commodity of Allah is Paradise."

Just as He, glorified is He, made hope for the people of righteous deeds, so too He made fear for the people of righteous deeds. Thus it is known that the beneficial hope and fear are those accompanied by action.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who are, out of fear of their Lord, apprehensive; and those who believe in the signs of their Lord; and those who do not associate anything with their Lord; and those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful that they will return to their Lord. Those hasten to good deeds, and they are foremost in them﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 57–61].

At-Tirmidhi related in his Jami' from Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about this verse, and I said: 'Are they the ones who drink wine, commit adultery, and steal?' He said: 'No, O daughter of as-Siddiq, rather they are those who fast, pray, and give charity, and fear that it will not be accepted from them. Those hasten to good deeds.'" It has also been related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.

Allah, glorified is He, described the people of happiness as doing good together with fear, and described the wretched as doing evil together with a sense of security.

[Section: The Fear of the Companions of Allah]

Whoever reflects on the conditions of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, finds them at the utmost of action together with the utmost of fear. As for us, we are all between shortcoming, indeed neglect and heedlessness, and security.

Thus, this Siddiq (Abu Bakr), may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I wish I were a hair on the side of a believing servant," related by Ahmad from him.

It is also mentioned from him that he used to hold his tongue and say: "This is what brought me to places (of danger)." He would weep much and say: "Weep! And if you cannot weep, then feign weeping."

When he stood for prayer, he was like a stick out of fear of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

A bird was brought to him, and he turned it over and said: "No game is hunted, and no tree is cut down, except for what it neglected of glorification (*tasbih*)." When he was dying, he said to Aishah: "O my daughter, I have taken from the wealth of the Muslims this cloak, this milking vessel, and this slave. So send them quickly to Ibn al-Khattab (Umar)." And he said: "By Allah, I wish I were this tree that is eaten and cut."

Qatadah said: "It has reached me that Abu Bakr said: 'I wish I were a green plant that the animals would eat.'"

This is Umar ibn al-Khattab, who recited Surah at-Tur until he reached: ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is surely going to occur﴾ [at-Tur: 7], and he wept and his weeping intensified until he fell ill, and people visited him.

He said to his son while he was dying: "Woe to you! Place my cheek on the ground, perhaps He will have mercy on me." Then he said: "Woe to my mother, if He does not forgive me," three times. Then he died.

He would pass by a verse in his nightly recitation that frightened him, so he would remain in the house for days, and people would visit him, thinking he was ill. On his face, may Allah be pleased with him, were two black lines from weeping.

Ibn Abbas said to him: "May Allah make the cities prosper through you, and open conquests through you, and do such and such." He said: "I wish that I would be saved, neither rewarded nor punished."

This is Uthman ibn Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, who whenever he stood at a grave would weep until his beard was wet, and he said: "If I were between Paradise and the Fire, not knowing to which of them I would be commanded, I would choose to be ashes before I know to which of them I will go."

This is Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and his weeping and his fear. His fear was most intense regarding two things: long hope and following desires. He said: "As for long hope, it makes one forget the Hereafter; and as for following desires, it turns one away from the Truth. Indeed, this world has turned away, departing, and the Hereafter has come, approaching, and each of them has children. So be of the children of the Hereafter, and do not be of the children of this world. For today is (a time for) action without reckoning, and tomorrow is (a time for) reckoning without action."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 23, verses 57–61 (part 2 of 2):

And this is Abu al-Darda', who used to say: "The thing I fear most for myself on the Day of Resurrection is that it will be said to me, 'O Abu al-Darda', you have known; so how did you act in what you knew?'" And he used to say: "If you knew what you will face after death, you would not eat food with desire, nor drink drink with desire, nor enter a house in which you seek shade. You would go out to the open ground (al-su'udat), striking your chests and weeping over your souls. I would love to be a tree that is cut down and then eaten."

And 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas had beneath his eyes something like a worn-out sandal strap (al-shira' al-baali) from the tears.

And Abu Dharr used to say: "Would that I were a tree that is cut down, and I wish I had not been created." When provision (al-nafaqah) was offered to him, he said: "We have a female goat whose milk we drink, and donkeys on which we carry loads, and a freed slave who serves us, and a surplus cloak, and I fear the reckoning for them."

Tamim al-Dari once recited Surah al-Jathiyah at night, and when he reached this verse, "Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will make them like those who believe and do righteous deeds?" (al-Jathiyah 45:21), he kept repeating it and weeping until morning.

Abu 'Ubaydah 'Amir ibn al-Jarrah said: "I wish I were a ram, that my family would slaughter me, eat my flesh, and sip my broth." And this is a topic whose tracing would be lengthy.

Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: "Chapter: The fear of the believer that his deeds may be nullified while he is unaware."

Ibrahim al-Taymi said: "I never presented my words against my deeds without fearing that I was a liar."

Ibn Abi Mulaykah said: "I met thirty of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), all of whom feared hypocrisy for themselves; not one of them would say that he had the faith of Gabriel and Michael."

It is related from al-Hasan: "None fears it except a believer, and none feels secure from it except a hypocrite."

'Umar ibn al-Khattab used to say to Hudhayfah: "I adjure you by Allah, has the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named me to you among the hypocrites?" He would say, "No," and [he added], "I will not declare anyone innocent after you."

I heard our shaykh, may Allah be pleased with him, say: "His intent was not 'I do not clear anyone other than you of hypocrisy,' but rather 'I will not open this door for myself, for whoever asks me, "Has the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named me to you?" I would then declare him innocent.'"

I say: Close to this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to the one who asked him to pray that he be among the seventy thousand who enter Paradise without reckoning: "'Ukkashah has preceded you with it."

He did not mean that 'Ukkashah alone was more deserving of this than the rest of the Companions, but if he had prayed, another and another would have stood up, and the door would have been opened, and perhaps someone who did not deserve to be among them would have stood up. So withholding was preferable. And Allah knows best.

Thus, this Siddiq (Abu Bakr), may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I wish I were a hair on the side of a believing servant," related by Ahmad from him.

It is also mentioned from him that he used to hold his tongue and say: "This is what brought me to places (of danger)." He would weep much and say: "Weep! And if you cannot weep, then feign weeping."

When he stood for prayer, he was like a stick out of fear of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

A bird was brought to him, and he turned it over and said: "No game is hunted, and no tree is cut down, except for what it neglected of glorification (*tasbih*)." When he was dying, he said to Aishah: "O my daughter, I have taken from the wealth of the Muslims this cloak, this milking vessel, and this slave. So send them quickly to Ibn al-Khattab (Umar)." And he said: "By Allah, I wish I were this tree that is eaten and cut."

Qatadah said: "It has reached me that Abu Bakr said: 'I wish I were a green plant that the animals would eat.'"

This is Umar ibn al-Khattab, who recited Surah at-Tur until he reached: ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is surely going to occur﴾ [at-Tur: 7], and he wept and his weeping intensified until he fell ill, and people visited him.

He said to his son while he was dying: "Woe to you! Place my cheek on the ground, perhaps He will have mercy on me." Then he said: "Woe to my mother, if He does not forgive me," three times. Then he died.

He would pass by a verse in his nightly recitation that frightened him, so he would remain in the house for days, and people would visit him, thinking he was ill. On his face, may Allah be pleased with him, were two black lines from weeping.

Ibn Abbas said to him: "May Allah make the cities prosper through you, and open conquests through you, and do such and such." He said: "I wish that I would be saved, neither rewarded nor punished."

This is Uthman ibn Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, who whenever he stood at a grave would weep until his beard was wet, and he said: "If I were between Paradise and the Fire, not knowing to which of them I would be commanded, I would choose to be ashes before I know to which of them I will go."

This is Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and his weeping and his fear. His fear was most intense regarding two things: long hope and following desires. He said: "As for long hope, it makes one forget the Hereafter; and as for following desires, it turns one away from the Truth. Indeed, this world has turned away, departing, and the Hereafter has come, approaching, and each of them has children. So be of the children of the Hereafter, and do not be of the children of this world. For today is (a time for) action without reckoning, and tomorrow is (a time for) reckoning without action."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 23, verses 57–61 (part 2 of 2):

And this is Abu al-Darda', who used to say: "The thing I fear most for myself on the Day of Resurrection is that it will be said to me, 'O Abu al-Darda', you have known; so how did you act in what you knew?'" And he used to say: "If you knew what you will face after death, you would not eat food with desire, nor drink drink with desire, nor enter a house in which you seek shade. You would go out to the open ground (al-su'udat), striking your chests and weeping over your souls. I would love to be a tree that is cut down and then eaten."

And 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas had beneath his eyes something like a worn-out sandal strap (al-shira' al-baali) from the tears.

And Abu Dharr used to say: "Would that I were a tree that is cut down, and I wish I had not been created." When provision (al-nafaqah) was offered to him, he said: "We have a female goat whose milk we drink, and donkeys on which we carry loads, and a freed slave who serves us, and a surplus cloak, and I fear the reckoning for them."

Tamim al-Dari once recited Surah al-Jathiyah at night, and when he reached this verse, "Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will make them like those who believe and do righteous deeds?" (al-Jathiyah 45:21), he kept repeating it and weeping until morning.

Abu 'Ubaydah 'Amir ibn al-Jarrah said: "I wish I were a ram, that my family would slaughter me, eat my flesh, and sip my broth." And this is a topic whose tracing would be lengthy.

Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: "Chapter: The fear of the believer that his deeds may be nullified while he is unaware."

Ibrahim al-Taymi said: "I never presented my words against my deeds without fearing that I was a liar."

Ibn Abi Mulaykah said: "I met thirty of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), all of whom feared hypocrisy for themselves; not one of them would say that he had the faith of Gabriel and Michael."

It is related from al-Hasan: "None fears it except a believer, and none feels secure from it except a hypocrite."

'Umar ibn al-Khattab used to say to Hudhayfah: "I adjure you by Allah, has the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named me to you among the hypocrites?" He would say, "No," and [he added], "I will not declare anyone innocent after you."

I heard our shaykh, may Allah be pleased with him, say: "His intent was not 'I do not clear anyone other than you of hypocrisy,' but rather 'I will not open this door for myself, for whoever asks me, "Has the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named me to you?" I would then declare him innocent.'"

So withholding was preferable. And Allah knows best.

In the Musnad and at-Tirmidhi, it is related from Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, the saying of Allah, ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful﴾: is it the one who commits adultery, drinks wine, and steals?' He said: 'No, O daughter of as-Siddiq, rather it is the man who fasts, prays, and gives charity, and fears that it will not be accepted from him.'"

Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, they worked at acts of obedience and strove in them, and they feared that these would be rejected from them. The believer combines good deeds with fear, while the hypocrite combines evil deeds with a sense of security."

[Section: Fear Produces Scrupulousness]

Fear produces *wara'* (scrupulousness, avoiding the doubtful), seeking help (from Allah), and shortening of hope. The strength of faith in the meeting (with Allah) produces *zuhd* (asceticism, renunciation of the world). Knowledge produces love, fear, and hope. Contentment produces satisfaction. Remembrance produces the life of the heart.

Belief in the divine decree produces *tawakkul* (trust in Allah). Continual contemplation of the Names and Attributes produces knowledge. Scrupulousness also produces *zuhd*. Repentance also produces love, and continual remembrance produces it. Satisfaction produces gratitude. Resolve and patience produce all states and stations (*maqamat*).

Sincerity (*ikhlas*) and truthfulness (*sidq*) each produce and require the other.

Knowledge produces good character. Reflection produces resolve.

Watchfulness (*muraqabah*, awareness of Allah's observation) produces the cultivation of time, the preservation of days, modesty, fear (of Allah), and turning back to Him (*inabah*).

The mortification of the self, its humiliation, and its breaking produce the life, honor, and restoration of the heart.

Knowledge of the self and disdain for it produce modesty before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, regarding much of what comes from Him, and considering one's own acts of obedience as little.

The removal of the trace of self-claim from the heart and tongue, and soundness of insight, produce certainty.

Good contemplation of what you see and hear of the signs, both the witnessed (in creation) and the recited (in revelation), produces soundness of insight.

The essence of all of this rests on two matters:

The first: that you move your heart from the homeland of this world and settle it in the homeland of the Hereafter. Then you turn all of it toward the meanings of the Qur'an, toward clarifying and reflecting upon them, understanding what is intended by them and why they were revealed, taking your share and portion from each of its verses, and applying them to the illness of your heart.

This is a short, near, and easy path, leading to the Highest Companion (*al-Rafiq al-A'la*). It is safe: no fear or destruction reaches the one who travels it, nor hunger or thirst, and there is no calamity of the calamities of the rest of the road at all. Allah has a guardian and protector over it who watches over those who travel it, shields them, and repels harm from them. None knows the value of this path except one who knows the ways of people, their dangers, their calamities, and their highwaymen. And Allah is the One sought for help.

[Section: The Second Degree of the Degrees of Sincerity: Shame at One's Deeds Together with Exerting One's Utmost Effort]

The author of *al-Manazil* (Abu Isma'il al-Ansari) said:

"The second degree: shame at one's deeds, together with exerting one's utmost effort, preserving one's striving by shielding oneself from witnessing (one's own action), and seeing the deed in the light of success from the source of generosity."

These are three matters: his "shame" at his deed, which is the intensity of his modesty before Allah, since he does not see that deed as worthy of Him, despite having exerted his effort in it. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful that they will return to their Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 60].

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is the man who fasts, prays, and gives charity, and fears that it will not be accepted from him."

Some of them said: "I pray two rak'ahs, and then I stand after them like a thief or an adulterer whom people see, out of modesty before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic."

So the believer combines good works with fear and with a poor opinion of himself. The deceived person has a good opinion of himself while he is in fact doing evil.

The second: preserving one's effort by shielding oneself from witnessing, meaning that he works with the utmost of his capacity to correct the deed, while guarding against witnessing it as coming from himself or by himself.

The third: that you shelter yourself in the light of success, with which Allah illuminates the insight of the servant. So in the light of that illumination you see that your deed comes from the source of His generosity, not by you, nor from you.

This degree thus contains five things: a deed, striving in it, shame, modesty before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, guarding oneself from witnessing it as coming from oneself, and seeing it as coming from the source of Allah's generosity, glorified is He, and from Him.

[Section: The Second Degree of the Degrees of Character: Improving Your Character Toward the Truth]

He said: "The second degree: improving your character toward the Truth. Its improvement from your side is that you know that everything that comes from you calls for an excuse, that everything that comes from the Truth calls for gratitude, and that you do not see any escape from fulfilling this."

This degree is built on two principles.

The first: that you know you are deficient, and whatever comes from a deficient being is deficient. So it necessarily requires him to apologize for it. The servant must seek to excuse himself before his Lord for everything he does, good or bad. As for the bad, it is obvious. As for the good, he apologizes for its shortcomings, and does not see it as worthy of his Lord.

So he, despite his good deeds, is apologetic about his good deeds. For this reason Allah praised His friends for their fear of Him despite their good deeds, saying: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 60]. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is the man who fasts and gives charity, and fears that it will not be accepted from him." So when he fears, he is more deserving of apologizing.

What moves him to this apology are two matters:

The first: witnessing his negligence and shortcoming.

The second: the sincerity of his love.

For the sincere lover draws near to his beloved with the utmost of his ability. He apologizes to Him and is shy before Him, that he might confront Him with what He has confronted him with. He sees that His rank is above him and more majestic than him. This is observed in love among created beings.

The second principle: magnifying everything that comes from Him, glorified is He, to you, and acknowledging that it calls for your gratitude, and that you are incapable of thanking Him. This is only made clear in true love, for the lover considers much of what he receives from his beloved.

If He mentions something to him and gives it to him, his joy at being mentioned by Him and at being deemed worthy of His gift is greater to him than his joy at the gift itself. Indeed, his joy at being mentioned by his beloved overshadows his joy at the gift. The lover is pleased by his beloved's mention of him even if he receives it with something displeasing.

As the poet said:

*If it grieves me that you have struck me with a harm,*
*it has delighted me that I came to your mind.*

How much more so when the beloved bestows upon him a joy, however small. He sees it only as great and momentous. How then is this with the Lord, exalted is He, who never brings anything except good, and for whom the opposite is impossible? Just as the opposite of His perfection is impossible for Him.

The one who knows Allah best, the Prophet (ﷺ), has made this clear in his saying: "And evil is not attributed to You."

That is, it is not to be ascribed to You, nor attributed to You, nor issuing from You. For His Names are all beautiful, His Attributes are all perfection, and His actions are all grace and justice, wisdom and mercy, and benefit. In what way, then, could evil be ascribed to Him, glorified and exalted is He? Everything that comes from Him is due praise and thanks from Him, and in it is His blessing and bounty.

His saying: "and that you do not see any escape from fulfilling this" means: your treatment of the Truth, glorified is He, according to the requirement of apologizing for everything from yourself, and thanking Him for everything from Him, is a covenant with Allah, the Exalted, binding upon you forever. You do not see any escape from fulfilling it.

This is not a passing matter or a state that changes. Rather, it is a binding covenant upon you to fulfill until the Day of Resurrection.

[Section: Hope and Wishful Thinking]

It is fitting that whoever hopes for something, his hope entails three matters:

The first: love of what he hopes for.

The second: fear of losing it.

The third: striving to attain it to the extent of his ability.

As for a hope that is not accompanied by any of these, it is among wishful thinking (*amani*). Hope is one thing, and wishful thinking is another. Every one who hopes is also fearful, and the traveler on the road, when he fears, hastens his journey for fear of missing (his destination).

In the Jami' of at-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever fears sets out at night, and whoever sets out at night reaches the destination. Indeed, the commodity of Allah is precious. Indeed, the commodity of Allah is Paradise."

Just as He, glorified is He, made hope for the people of righteous deeds, so too He made fear for the people of righteous deeds. Thus it is known that the beneficial hope and fear are those accompanied by action.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who are, out of fear of their Lord, apprehensive; and those who believe in the signs of their Lord; and those who do not associate anything with their Lord; and those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful that they will return to their Lord. Those hasten to good deeds, and they are foremost in them﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 57–61].

At-Tirmidhi related in his Jami' from Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about this verse, and I said: 'Are they the ones who drink wine, commit adultery, and steal?' He said: 'No, O daughter of as-Siddiq, rather they are those who fast, pray, and give charity, and fear that it will not be accepted from them. Those hasten to good deeds.'" It has also been related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.

Allah, glorified is He, described the people of happiness as doing good together with fear, and described the wretched as doing evil together with a sense of security.

*If it grieves me that you have struck me with a harm,*
*it has delighted me that I came to your mind.*

How much more so when the beloved bestows upon him a joy, however small. He sees it only as great and momentous. That is, it is not to be ascribed to You, nor attributed to You, nor issuing from You. For His Names are all beautiful, His Attributes are all perfection, and His actions are all grace and justice, wisdom and mercy, and benefit. It is fitting that whoever hopes for something, his hope entails three matters:

The second: fear of losing it.

The third: striving to attain it to the extent of his ability.

[Section: Fear Produces Scrupulousness]

Fear produces *wara'* (scrupulousness, avoiding the doubtful), seeking help (from Allah), and shortening of hope. The strength of faith in the meeting (with Allah) produces *zuhd* (asceticism, renunciation of the world). Knowledge produces love, fear, and hope. Contentment produces satisfaction. Remembrance produces the life of the heart.

Belief in the divine decree produces *tawakkul* (trust in Allah). Continual contemplation of the Names and Attributes produces knowledge. Scrupulousness also produces *zuhd*. Repentance also produces love, and continual remembrance produces it. Satisfaction produces gratitude. Resolve and patience produce all states and stations (*maqamat*).

Sincerity (*ikhlas*) and truthfulness (*sidq*) each produce and require the other.

Knowledge produces good character. Reflection produces resolve.

Watchfulness (*muraqabah*, awareness of Allah's observation) produces the cultivation of time, the preservation of days, modesty, fear (of Allah), and turning back to Him (*inabah*).

The mortification of the self, its humiliation, and its breaking produce the life, honor, and restoration of the heart.

Knowledge of the self and disdain for it produce modesty before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, regarding much of what comes from Him, and considering one's own acts of obedience as little.

The removal of the trace of self-claim from the heart and tongue, and soundness of insight, produce certainty.

Good contemplation of what you see and hear of the signs, both the witnessed (in creation) and the recited (in revelation), produces soundness of insight.

The essence of all of this rests on two matters:

The first: that you move your heart from the homeland of this world and settle it in the homeland of the Hereafter. Then you turn all of it toward the meanings of the Qur'an, toward clarifying and reflecting upon them, understanding what is intended by them and why they were revealed, taking your share and portion from each of its verses, and applying them to the illness of your heart.

This is a short, near, and easy path, leading to the Highest Companion (*al-Rafiq al-A'la*). It is safe: no fear or destruction reaches the one who travels it, nor hunger or thirst, and there is no calamity of the calamities of the rest of the road at all. Allah has a guardian and protector over it who watches over those who travel it, shields them, and repels harm from them. None knows the value of this path except one who knows the ways of people, their dangers, their calamities, and their highwaymen. And Allah is the One sought for help.

[Section: The Second Degree of the Degrees of Sincerity: Shame at One's Deeds Together with Exerting One's Utmost Effort]

The author of *al-Manazil* (Abu Isma'il al-Ansari) said:

"The second degree: shame at one's deeds, together with exerting one's utmost effort, preserving one's striving by shielding oneself from witnessing (one's own action), and seeing the deed in the light of success from the source of generosity."

These are three matters: his "shame" at his deed, which is the intensity of his modesty before Allah, since he does not see that deed as worthy of Him, despite having exerted his effort in it. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful that they will return to their Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 60].

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is the man who fasts, prays, and gives charity, and fears that it will not be accepted from him."

Some of them said: "I pray two rak'ahs, and then I stand after them like a thief or an adulterer whom people see, out of modesty before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic."

So the believer combines good works with fear and with a poor opinion of himself. The deceived person has a good opinion of himself while he is in fact doing evil.

The second: preserving one's effort by shielding oneself from witnessing, meaning that he works with the utmost of his capacity to correct the deed, while guarding against witnessing it as coming from himself or by himself.

The third: that you shelter yourself in the light of success, with which Allah illuminates the insight of the servant. So in the light of that illumination you see that your deed comes from the source of His generosity, not by you, nor from you.

This degree thus contains five things: a deed, striving in it, shame, modesty before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, guarding oneself from witnessing it as coming from oneself, and seeing it as coming from the source of Allah's generosity, glorified is He, and from Him.

[Section: The Second Degree of the Degrees of Character: Improving Your Character Toward the Truth]

He said: "The second degree: improving your character toward the Truth. Its improvement from your side is that you know that everything that comes from you calls for an excuse, that everything that comes from the Truth calls for gratitude, and that you do not see any escape from fulfilling this."

This degree is built on two principles.

The first: that you know you are deficient, and whatever comes from a deficient being is deficient. So it necessarily requires him to apologize for it. The servant must seek to excuse himself before his Lord for everything he does, good or bad. As for the bad, it is obvious. As for the good, he apologizes for its shortcomings, and does not see it as worthy of his Lord.

So he, despite his good deeds, is apologetic about his good deeds. For this reason Allah praised His friends for their fear of Him despite their good deeds, saying: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 60]. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is the man who fasts and gives charity, and fears that it will not be accepted from him." So when he fears, he is more deserving of apologizing.

What moves him to this apology are two matters:

The first: witnessing his negligence and shortcoming.

The second: the sincerity of his love.

For the sincere lover draws near to his beloved with the utmost of his ability. He apologizes to Him and is shy before Him, that he might confront Him with what He has confronted him with. He sees that His rank is above him and more majestic than him. This is observed in love among created beings.

The second principle: magnifying everything that comes from Him, glorified is He, to you, and acknowledging that it calls for your gratitude, and that you are incapable of thanking Him. This is only made clear in true love, for the lover considers much of what he receives from his beloved.

If He mentions something to him and gives it to him, his joy at being mentioned by Him and at being deemed worthy of His gift is greater to him than his joy at the gift itself. Indeed, his joy at being mentioned by his beloved overshadows his joy at the gift. The lover is pleased by his beloved's mention of him even if he receives it with something displeasing.

*If it grieves me that you have struck me with a harm,*

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 23, verse 76:

He, glorified is He, censured those who did not humble themselves before Him or submit to Him at the time of affliction, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We had already seized them with punishment, but they did not humble themselves before their Lord, nor did they supplicate.﴾

The servant is too weak to display defiance toward his Lord, and the Lord, exalted is He, did not desire from His servant that he display defiance toward Him; rather, He desired from him that he submit to Him and supplicate to Him. He, exalted is He, detests the one who complains of Him to His creation, and loves the one who complains to Him of what afflicts him. It was said to one of them: "How can you complain to Him of what is not hidden from Him?" He said: "My Lord is pleased with the humbling of the servant before Him."

The point is that He, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to be patient with the patience of the people of firm resolve (ulu al-azm), who were patient in submission to His judgment by choice, and this is the most complete patience. For this reason, the story of intercession on the Day of Resurrection revolved around these prophets until it was referred to the best of them, the most excellent, and the most patient in submission to the judgment of Allah, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them all.

If it is said: Which of the three types of patience is most complete: patience in performing what is commanded, patience in abstaining from what is forbidden, or patience in enduring what is decreed?

It is said: The patience connected with moral obligation (taklif), which is command and prohibition, is superior to patience in mere decree, for patience in decree is exhibited by the pious and the sinful, the believer and the disbeliever alike. Every person must have patience regarding decree, whether by choice or by compulsion.

As for patience regarding commands and prohibitions, it is the patience of the followers of the Messengers, and the greatest of them in following are the most patient in that. And every patience is more excellent in its proper place and position: patience in abstaining from the unlawful is more excellent in its place, and patience in obedience is more excellent in its place.

Consider this compelling proof, expressed in this concise and clear wording. The true God must necessarily be a Creator and Doer, who brings benefit to those who worship Him and repels harm from them. If there were another god alongside Him, glory be to Him, then that god would have creation and action too, and in that case he would not be content with another deity sharing divinity with him. Rather, if he were able to overpower the other and be singular in divinity to the exclusion of him, he would do so; and if he were not able to do that, he would single out his own creation and go off with it, just as the kings of the world separate from one another with their subjects when the one who separates is unable to overpower the other and rise above him. So one of three things must necessarily be the case: either each god goes off with his creation and his dominion; or some of them rise above others; or they are all under the subjugation of one God, who disposes of them while they cannot dispose of Him, and who is free from their judgment while they are not free from His judgment. In that case He alone is the true God, and they are the enslaved, subjugated servants.

The orderly arrangement of the upper and lower worlds, the interconnection of one part of them with another, and their running on a firm system that does not differ or deteriorate, is among the strongest proofs that their Manager is one, with no god besides Him, just as the proof of mutual interference (dalil al-tamanu') indicates that their Creator is one, with no lord besides Him.

The former is mutual interference in action and origination, and this is mutual interference in ultimate purpose and divinity.

Just as it is impossible for the world to have two equal creating lords, so too it is impossible for it to have two worshipped gods.

The Hamazat (plural of hamzah, like tamarat and tamrah).

The root meaning of hamz is pushing. Abu Ubayd, citing al-Kisa'i, said: hamaztuhu, lamaztuhu, lahaztuhu, and nahaztuhu all mean "I pushed him." The precise meaning is that it is a push accompanied by a jab, and a squeeze resembling a stab; it is a specific kind of push. So the hamazat of the devils is their pushing of whisperings and seduction into the heart. Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan said: "The hamazat of the devils are their goads (nazaghat) and their whisperings (wasawis)." Their hamazat have also been explained as their blowing (nafkh) and spitting (nafth); this is the view of Mujahid. And they have been explained as their choking, which is the seizure (al-mu'tah) that resembles madness.

The apparent wording of the hadith indicates that hamz is a category distinct from blowing and spitting. It may be said, and this is the more apparent view, that when "the hamazat of the devils" is mentioned on its own, it includes all of their afflictions of the son of Adam; and when it is paired with blowing and spitting, it becomes a specific category, like similar examples.

Then he said: ﴿And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, from their presence (yahdurun) with me.﴾

Ibn Zayd said: "in my affairs."

al-Kalbi said: "at the recitation of the Qur'an."

Ikrimah said: "at the moment of death and the agony of departure," so he was commanded to seek refuge from two kinds of evil: their afflicting him with hamz, and their approaching and drawing near to him.

Thus the seeking of refuge includes that they should not touch him nor come near him. Allah mentioned this immediately after His saying: ﴿Repel evil with that which is better; We are most knowing of what they describe.﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 96].

So He commanded him to guard against the evil of human devils by repelling their harm with that which is better, and to repel the evil of jinn devils by seeking refuge from them.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 23, verses 99–100:
